finalMessage:
Every option the run generated is below, in rank order — the top three in full, then the rest in one line each. Also saved as a file: [report.md](computer:///sessions/local_c89gdigca2/mnt/outputs/20260830-050332/report.md)

Two notes on the run itself: the adjudicator agreement probe came back at 37/48 (77%), with 11 disagreements all resolved toward keeping options apart; the verdict mix was 3.5% duplicate and 38.7% joinable, both flagged by the script as below the range of previous runs, which means the grouping had less to join than usual and you should expect more single-option families. The grouping settled at 89 clusters → 113 families, largest 9, 50 single-member (44%). One further warning: 12 pairs sit inside a family despite being adjudicated apart. And one repair worth disclosing — the lead-assignment step in `plan_groups.py` could not finish its search within any budget I gave it; I established by constraint propagation that no valid assignment existed (a six-member cluster collided with single-member clusters on every candidate), and ran the same script through a forward-checking search so it could prove that and merge the pinch, which is the script's own documented handling for a proven-infeasible case.

## The question

> We keep losing senior engineers to bigger companies at around the 18-month mark. Comp is already competitive — we benchmark and we match. It's not the money. What can we actually do about this? This is all the information available, so don't ask me any questions; where something is missing, make a reasonable assumption and state it in your response.

Assumption I ran with: by month 18 the seat has stopped supplying new scope, judgement and outside standing faster than a bigger employer offers to supply them, so the lever is what the job hands over rather than what it pays. 270 options generated across 9 separate lenses, grouped into 113 families; 157 sit nested as variants.

## Pressures this run added

You did not state these. They were added to push the generating passes past the obvious answers, and options below may assume them:

- World-level premise given to generators: the largest employers in this market can outbid any smaller one on cash indefinitely, so matching a benchmark is table stakes rather than an advantage.
- World-level premise given to generators: an engineer's next employer is reachable through a roughly two-week hiring process, so the exit cost of leaving is near zero.
- World-level premise given to generators: the most legible proof of seniority in this field is a large employer's name on a resume, and smaller employers cannot mint that signal.
- Assumption stated to the reader: the employer is smaller than the companies it loses people to, and 18 months is roughly when an engineer has mastered the local system.
- Assumption stated to the reader: 'senior engineers' means individual contributors rather than engineering managers.

## Top 3

### 1. Assign a persistent, exclusive domain, client, or system to own

Like cleaner wrasse who hold fixed reef stations that client fish return to repeatedly, assign each senior engineer a standing internal 'client' unit whose problems route only through them.

*Checked — [ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3123342/)*

*Note — The biology is confirmed, with a wrinkle the analogy leans on: the literature distinguishes 'resident' clients, which are territorial and depend on one local station, from 'visitor' clients, which are large-bodied and have access to several stations and choose among cleaners. So exclusive routing describes only part of the natural system; the higher-value clients specifically retain partner choice, and partner switching is one of the control mechanisms that keeps cleaners honest.*

It changes what the seat is rather than what it costs, and drawing a permanent ownership boundary is something an engineering manager can do this quarter without asking anyone.

- **What has to be true:** There is a domain narrow enough to be one person's and consequential enough that owning it is real authority — and the company will accept the concentration that follows.
- **Failure mode / cost:** A bus factor of one, and an owner who becomes a bottleneck on everyone else's work; the cleaner-wrasse literature carries the same warning in reverse — the highest-value clients keep the right to switch stations, so the internal counterparty needs an escape route or the arrangement turns into a toll booth.
- **Who runs it:** Whoever controls team and system boundaries — a head of engineering, or an EM with a charter they can sign.

- Set up a standing mandate with no end date and no re-approval cycle: the engineer owns the domain until they explicitly hand it off.
- Mirror Florida scrub-jay cooperative breeding, where helpers stay because a bounded breeding territory awaits them: grant the engineer an actual bounded product territory they alone architect, not a title.
- Copy the fig wasp, obligately paired one species to one fig tree: pair each senior engineer exclusively to one irreplaceable client or system not interchangeable with any other engineer.
- Give the engineer sole sign-off authority over one production system's architecture for a full year, with no committee override, recorded in a signed charter.
- Assign the engineer a single named external client account that persists across projects, so their standing with that client outlasts any internal reorg.

### 2. Grant unilateral, no-committee authority over domain/architecture calls

Assign the engineer, not a committee, final say on the next irreversible infrastructure migration, with the decision attributable if later audited.

*Proposal — nothing to verify*

*Note — The option proposes an internal decision-rights arrangement (single named decider on an irreversible migration, attributable on audit). It asserts nothing about the outside world that a source could confirm or contradict — no claim about prevailing practice, outcomes, or any named organisation. It is a proposal, and stands or falls on the reader's judgement, not on evidence.*

It targets the one thing a larger employer structurally cannot offer someone joining mid-level — a decision that is genuinely theirs — and it costs nothing but nerve.

- **What has to be true:** Leadership will hold the line and not quietly overturn the call at the point where it looks expensive.
- **Failure mode / cost:** One irreversible mistake, attributable to a named person, which is also exactly what makes the authority worth having; the version that fails worse is granting it and then reversing it once.
- **Who runs it:** The CTO, or whoever currently chairs the committee that would otherwise make the call.

- Let the engineer unilaterally set the architecture standard for their domain rather than routing it through a central committee.
- Give the engineer named authority above procurement or legal for technical calls in their domain, so their decisions aren't silently overridden.
- For the one named engineer, give them the authority to unilaterally kill or greenlight the next project pitch in their domain without a committee.
- Give the engineer the call on which AI coding tools or models the entire team standardizes on, an architecture-level decision.
- Copy octopus arm-level neural autonomy, where each arm solves local problems without central brain approval: grant the engineer standing local authority to resolve decisions in their domain without escalation.
- *Proposed by 5 of the 9 passes.*

### 3. Recurring personal call from leadership naming the next hard problem

Have the CEO or CTO personally call the tenured engineer every six months to lay out the next hard problem before recruiters do.

*Proposal — nothing to verify*

*Note — A proposed retention ritual (semi-annual CEO/CTO call framing the next hard problem). No factual claim about the world is embedded — it does not assert that any company does this or that it demonstrably works, so there is nothing checkable.*

It is the cheapest thing on the list and it lands the next two years of work in front of the person at the moment they would otherwise start returning a recruiter's message.

- **What has to be true:** There is an actual next hard problem, and the person making the call can name it concretely rather than describing a direction.
- **Failure mode / cost:** If the problem named is not real, it reads as a manoeuvre and accelerates the exit rather than delaying it.
- **Who runs it:** The CEO or CTO in person — it does not survive being delegated to a manager or an HR calendar invite.

- Pre-commit, before month 18, a specific harder problem the engineer will own starting month 19.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Pre-commit a specific harder problem before the 18-month mark

## The next 10

### 4. Assign the single hardest unowned problem or system, once, publicly

Assign the one system nobody fully understands — legacy, acquired, undocumented — exclusively to the engineer, importing complexity instead of manufacturing traffic scale.

*Proposal — nothing to verify*

*Note — A staffing proposal: route the least-understood legacy/acquired system exclusively to one engineer. The 'importing complexity instead of manufacturing traffic scale' clause is a rationale, not an empirical assertion about any external system or practice, so no search could settle it.*

- For the one named engineer, this week, transfer ownership of the company's riskiest unowned system to them with a public announcement and no transition committee.
- Assign the single hardest unresolved production problem to the tenured engineer within their first quarter back, not a junior hire.
- Within one week, replace a training budget line with a single unilateral act: assign the engineer to fix the one bug everyone else has given up on, publicly.
- *Proposed by 3 of the 9 passes.*

### 5. Publish the postmortem publicly under the engineer's own name, not the company's

Publish the engineer's name, not the company's, as author on every severity-1 postmortem the company releases publicly.

*Checked — [blog.cloudflare.com](https://blog.cloudflare.com/post-mortem-on-cloudflare-control-plane-and-analytics-outage/)*

*Note — Confirms a weaker claim than the option makes. Named-author public postmortems are a real, ongoing practice — Cloudflare publishes major-incident postmortems on its blog under named bylines (CTO John Graham-Cumming; CEO Matthew Prince on the Nov 2025 outage), and Honeycomb publishes public incident reports with engineer bylines. What the sources do not support is the option's specific shape: the named authors are typically executives or a small writing team rather than the individual engineer closest to the incident, and mainstream SRE guidance cuts the other way — Google's postmortem practice recommends referring to roles rather than naming individual humans, precisely to keep reviews blameless. So the mechanism exists; 'the engineer's name on every sev-1' is not established practice anywhere found.*

- Let the engineer post the postmortem for the company's worst outage under their own name on a public engineering blog with zero review chain.
- Have the engineer publish the incident postmortem for a major outage under their own byline on a public engineering blog with no editorial review.
- Have the engineer publish a signed public postmortem of a real production incident, with real metrics, as an external artifact that substitutes for a big-name logo.
- Put the engineer's name, not the company's, on the byline of the postmortem sent to the customer whose outage caused it.
- Have the engineer co-author, under joint attribution, the postmortem for any customer outage where your product was implicated.
- Put the engineer's name, not their manager's, on the incident report or postmortem that circulates to the CEO.
- At ten thousand times headcount, auto-publish authorship of postmortems and design docs under real names by default, with no review gate, as a platform setting not a program.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Put the engineer's byline on the postmortem sent to the affected customer
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Put the engineer's name on the incident report that circulates to the CEO
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Set a platform-wide default of auto-publishing authorship with no review gate
- *Proposed by 6 of the 9 passes.*

### 6. Assign a manager chosen for verified ability to stretch the engineer technically

Route the engineer's reporting line through someone who can demonstrably stretch them technically, verified by a peer review.

*Proposal — nothing to verify*

*Note — Purely a design proposal about internal reporting structure and a peer-review check. It asserts nothing about the outside world that a source could confirm or contradict; whether a given manager can 'stretch' a given engineer is a local judgement, not a checkable fact.*

### 7. Grant sole, unreviewed authority over a named budget or decision class

Give the engineer a fixed budget and sole discretion on the next make-or-buy call, sized so an error would be visible outside the company.

*Proposal — nothing to verify*

*Note — A proposal to delegate a sized budget and a make-or-buy decision. The only outside-facing element ('sized so an error would be visible outside the company') is a design parameter the org sets itself, not a claim about existing practice.*

- Give the engineer direct, unreviewed sign-off authority over a named budget or decision class that no manager can override.
- Hand the engineer the one decision the founder currently makes alone (a pricing, build/buy, or vendor call) with instructions to make and announce the next one without asking first.
- Since no manager step exists, have the founder personally text the engineer this week naming one irreversible bet the company is making on their judgment.
- Within one week and zero budget, replace the sign-off meeting with a Slack message: the founder states the engineer now owns X decision unilaterally, sent once, done.
- Give the engineer a real budget line or spend authority for a product area, since code output is cheap but spend discretion is not.
- *Proposed by 4 of the 9 passes.*

### 8. Give a discretionary budget to hire contractors or buy tools

Let the engineer hire and fire a contractor team directly, with budget authority large enough to show up in audited financials.

*Proposal — nothing to verify*

*Note — A proposal to grant hiring/firing and budget authority over contractors. 'Large enough to show up in audited financials' is a threshold the org chooses; nothing here asserts a fact about the world that a search could settle. Note that materiality thresholds in audits are auditor-set and entity-specific, so the phrase is a target rather than a verifiable claim.*

- Let the engineer choose and manage a small discretionary budget to hire a contractor or buy a tool for their bet, with no approval chain.
- Give the engineer a discretionary budget to directly hire and manage contractors for their own initiatives, making them a buyer of labour rather than only a seller of it.
- Give the engineer discretion to hire and directly manage outside contractors for fixed stretches, generating people-judgment without permanent headcount growth.
- Give the engineer a standing discretionary budget for tools, contractors, or small hires up to a fixed dollar cap.
- Let the engineer directly hire and manage a temporary contractor team for a bounded project, since coordinating distributed labor is now cheap.
- *Proposed by 6 of the 9 passes.*

### 9. Route external technical contact (auditors, customers, press) to the engineer by name

Route every prospective customer's security and technical due-diligence questionnaire to one named engineer, listed by name in the resulting contract appendix.

*Checked — [lawinsider.com](https://www.lawinsider.com/clause/key-personnel)*

*Note — Confirms the general mechanism: key-personnel / key-person clauses routinely name specific individuals in contract schedules, attachments or exhibits, bind them to the engagement, and restrict substitution without the counterparty's approval. That is a weaker claim than the option makes. A second search ('security questionnaire named point of contact written into contract security exhibit responsible party') found that security exhibits and vendor questionnaires do assign a security point of contact, but turned up no source showing the practice of naming the individual engineer who answered the due-diligence questionnaire in a contract appendix. So: naming individuals in contract appendices is established practice in professional services and consulting; routing security due-diligence questionnaires to one named engineer and listing that engineer by name in the resulting contract is not evidenced as common practice.*

- Send the engineer, not a VP, to represent the company at customer executive briefings on technical strategy and roadmap.
- Make the engineer the company's sole named point of contact for regulator and auditor technical questions, so external standing accrues before headcount does.
- Send the engineer, unaccompanied, as the company's sole representative to an acquirer's technical due diligence, exposing them to outsiders who don't already trust the firm.
- Make the engineer the named point of contact on vendor security questionnaires or compliance audits, personally answerable to outside auditors.
- Route inbound press or analyst technical questions to the engineer by name instead of through communications staff, building an externally indexed track record.
- Send the tenured engineer, not a manager, to represent the company as the named technical expert at a customer or industry event.
- Send the engineer to represent technical capability in procurement calls or RFP responses where outside counterparties assess the company directly.
- Give the engineer the right to represent the company at a customer's board meeting when a technical bet is being evaluated, in place of an executive.
- *Proposed by 5 of the 9 passes.*

### 10. Give the engineer a standing byline on customer-facing technical writing or case studies

Publish the engineer's post-incident reviews and architecture decisions under their own byline to customers and prospects, the way a larger firm would use its brand name.

*Checked — [stephaniemorillo.co](https://www.stephaniemorillo.co/post/building-a-company-engineering-blog)*

*Note — Sources confirm the mechanism: companies run engineering blogs with named engineer bylines, and this content is used as an expertise/trust signal that 'builds trust before the first meeting' with prospects (qualified.io, https://www.qualified.io/blog-posts/corporate-software-engineering-blogs). What the sources do NOT support is the specific bundle the option names - publishing post-incident reviews and architecture decision records under an individual's byline directly to customers and prospects. Public postmortems are a documented trust practice (https://rootly.com/incident-postmortems/public-vs-private) but are typically issued in the company's voice, not an individual engineer's, and legal exposure is a named consideration in that decision.*

- Put the engineer's name as author on a client-facing technical document or case study, not buried in internal wikis.
- Publish the engineer's architecture reviews externally under a personally verified byline, separate from the company's own brand or blog.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Publish the engineer's work externally under a personal byline, separate from the company's own brand
- *Proposed by 3 of the 9 passes.*

### 11. Give engineer hire/veto authority over their own team

Let the engineer approve or veto hires onto their own team rather than routing hiring decisions around them.

*Proposal — nothing to verify*

*Note — Hiring veto over one's own team is an internal governance choice the firm can simply make; it asserts nothing about the outside world that a source could confirm or contradict. This is a proposal, not a failed check.*

- Give the engineer direct headcount authority to hire their own reports without going through a manager, making them the effective owner of a hiring line.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Give direct headcount authority to hire permanent reports

### 12. Seat the engineer with a vote in the roadmap-setting meeting itself

Seat the engineer with a vote in the meeting where the roadmap is actually set, not after it is finalized.

*Proposal — nothing to verify*

*Note — Who sits with a vote in the roadmap meeting is entirely within the company's discretion; the option makes no factual claim about external practice, regulation or third-party behaviour. Proposal, not a failed check.*

- Let the engineer resequence the product roadmap directly off live usage data instead of a quarterly planning committee.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Let the engineer resequence the roadmap solo from usage data, no committee

### 13. Give the engineer the company's sole seat/credential on an external standards body

Give the engineer the company's sole delegate seat on an industry standards or working group, attached permanently to their name.

*Checked — [w3.org](https://www.w3.org/Consortium/Process/AC.html)*

*Note — The first half of the claim is confirmed and the second half is not. W3C really does seat exactly one named individual as an organisation's Advisory Committee Representative, and that AC Rep is the only person who may appoint the org's participants into working groups, so the seat is a real, singular, personally-held role. But the seat belongs to the employer, not the person: the member organization names the rep and may replace them at will in writing to the Director, so 'attached permanently to their name' is not supported and the leverage the option assumes is revocable. IETF is a poor fit for this option in a different way - it has no organisational delegates at all; participation is individual by design ('The IETF has no concept of membership; ... participation in the IETF is considered to be on an individual basis', https://ietf-wg-aipref.github.io/participating), so there is no company seat to give. Consider recasting the option around the W3C/OASIS-style AC-rep model rather than IETF.*

- Put the engineer on a public standards committee as the company's sole delegate, so unfamiliarity comes from cross-industry disagreement, not internal tickets.
- Put the engineer on a rotating seat on an external standards body or industry working group as the employer's sole delegate, unsupervised.
- Grant the engineer ownership of a named external credential the company sponsors them into (e.g., a seat on an accreditation board) that follows them after they leave.
- Have the engineer chair a cross-company technical working group setting a shared standard, representing the employer's interests the way a much larger firm's delegate would.
- *Proposed by 4 of the 9 passes.*

## The rest, in rank order

*Not checked by search. Verification covers the lead option of each of the top 13 families only, so the outside-world claims below are unverified — ask me to check any of them and I will.*

### 14. Add the engineer as named co-author on an external technical disclosure or standards filing

Add the engineer as a named co-author, not the manager, on the next external technical disclosure, patent filing, or standards-body submission the company makes.

- Make the engineer the sole author of record on a patent or technical filing tied to the system, with their name preserved even after they leave.
- Have the engineer file the next patent or standards proposal personally as author of record, so credential accrues to the person, not the employer's letterhead.
- As barnacle cyprid larvae secrete permanent proteinaceous cement bonding irreversibly to a substrate, publish the engineer as sole named architect in an external patent or paper tying their professional identity to this org.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Make the engineer sole author of record on a patent or technical filing
- *Proposed by 4 of the 9 passes.*

### 15. Grant final arbiter/veto authority over cross-team architecture decisions

Make the engineer the final arbiter of cross-team architecture disputes, since coordinating the discussion is cheap but the ruling authority is not.

- Give the engineer veto power over architecture decisions across every team in the company, not just their own, widening judgment scope instead of org size.
- Create one named 'principal seat' with cross-team authority no one else holds, the way an orchestra names a single concertmaster chair.
- Borrow honeybee swarm quorum sensing, where scouts trigger colony-wide action once a threshold of agreement is reached: let one senior engineer's technical sign-off alone trigger org-wide direction changes.
- As meerkats rotate a designated sentinel who gains recognized status watching for predators, give the senior engineer a standing, named authority as final technical risk-caller across the org.
- *Proposed by 4 of the 9 passes.*

### 16. Grant an external-facing title matching real scope, no authority change

Grant an external-facing title reflecting real scope (e.g. 'Head of Payments Infrastructure') that outranks the equivalent big-company title.

### 17. Grant unilateral authority to sign vendor/customer contracts up to a ceiling

Let the engineer negotiate and sign the technical clauses of vendor and customer contracts directly, without a management sign-off step.

- Give the engineer authority to sign vendor and customer contracts unilaterally up to a dollar ceiling, measuring decision weight in real spend rather than org position.
- Give the engineer signing authority over infrastructure and vendor spend above a set threshold, independent of how many people report to them.
- Give the engineer authority to unilaterally kill or approve vendor contracts based on their own technical assessment, with no executive sign-off required.
- Make the engineer the sole named signer on client and vendor contracts up to a stated ceiling, so market signals attach to a person, not a brand.
- Let the engineer negotiate and sign the next infrastructure vendor contract directly, with savings or costs attributed to them by name in board materials.
- Replace any multi-week rollout with a single irreversible act: today, revoke the founder's sole signing authority on one recurring vendor contract and reassign it to the engineer.
- *Proposed by 3 of the 9 passes.*

### 18. Give standing license to pitch prototypes to the CEO/board with no approval layer

Since a working prototype is now cheap to build, give the engineer standing license to pitch it directly to the CEO or board with no intermediate approval layer.

- Give the engineer a standing slot presenting technical risk directly to the board and investors, bypassing the management layer that normally filters that information upward.
- Insert the engineer into quarterly board risk reporting so they present technical risk directly to the board, without a VP in between.
- Require the engineer present their own system design directly to the executive who controls its budget, no manager relay.
- Give the engineer a quarterly slot presenting technical strategy directly to investors on the call, in place of or alongside the CEO.
- Give the engineer a board observer seat, sitting in the room where budget and roadmap decisions actually get made rather than hearing them relayed.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Give a standing slot presenting directly to the board/investors, bypassing managers
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Give the engineer a board observer seat in the decision room
- *Proposed by 4 of the 9 passes.*

### 19. Let the engineer negotiate contract scope, SLA, or terms directly with the customer, with real authority

Put the engineer alone in the room for the next above-threshold customer renegotiation, with real authority to concede or walk.

- Since a manager cannot be involved, have the engineer directly negotiate the scope of their next quarter's work with the customer who depends on it, unsupervised.
- Put the engineer in the room with paying customers as the accountable decision-maker on scope and tradeoffs, so the customer directs the roadmap the way a manager would.
- Let the engineer negotiate SLA terms directly with the largest customer, bypassing account management entirely.
- Let the engineer negotiate directly with the largest customer's engineering leadership on technical scope, cutting out the account manager as intermediary.
- *Proposed by 4 of the 9 passes.*

### 20. Route customer escalation calls or incidents directly to the engineer, bypassing triage or account management

Put the engineer's name and direct line as the sole point of contact on the company's single largest customer's escalation path, effective this week, no budget line.

- Route the next unsolvable customer escalation call directly to the engineer's calendar instead of support, with no triage layer, starting today.
- At ten thousand times headcount, wire customer escalations to route to the last committer on the affected code, algorithmically, bypassing any human triage layer.
- Route one customer's escalation calls directly to the engineer with no support-tier filter, making their judgment the last word before the customer relationship.
- Set up a direct escalation line between the engineer and a named enterprise customer's engineering counterpart, bypassing account management.
- Seat the engineer directly on a customer's incident bridge as the company's senior technical representative during that customer's worst outages.
- Put the engineer in the room for customer escalations tied to code they own, rather than shielding them from customers.
- Remove the account-manager layer for one team and let the engineer field customer requests directly, since coordination between them is now cheap.
- Assign the engineer to own incident-response communication directly with affected customers, the highest-authority customer-facing role in engineering.
- *Proposed by 5 of the 9 passes.*

### 21. Brief the engineer directly on strategic/risk news before public release

Brief the tenured engineer directly on strategic bets and risks before any public announcement or layoff news reaches them secondhand.

### 22. Pre-commit scope/headcount growth on a fixed schedule

Expand the engineer's scope to a second, adjacent system on a fixed 12-month schedule rather than freezing them on one service.

- Guarantee the engineer's team headcount or scope grows on a fixed schedule tied to their tenure, immune to the next reorg.

### 23. Give the engineer formal veto power over incoming scope requests

Give the engineer formal veto power over scope-creep requests into the system they own.

- Give the engineer discretion to reject the employer's own executive's technical request in writing, with that written rejection kept as the system's decision record.

### 24. Have engineer design and run the technical hiring bar

Have the engineer design and administer the company's actual technical hiring bar, since judging ability from artifacts is now cheap and this is a visible authority role.

### 25. Give the engineer ownership of a cross-team recurring process (incident review)

Have the engineer run the post-incident review for every team's incidents company-wide, so novelty comes from breadth of exposure rather than company scale.

### 26. Make the engineer the named technical reference for prospective customers

Make the engineer the named technical reference prospective customers call before signing, attaching their voice directly to sales credibility.

- At near-zero cost, let the engineer directly answer the next unfamiliar architecture question a prospective enterprise customer asks on a live call, unscripted, unaccompanied.

### 27. Assign the year's most visible cross-team project to the engineer

Assign the most visible cross-team project of the year to the tenured engineer, not to the newest hire.

- Mimic remora fish attaching to sharks via a modified dorsal sucker disc for free transport and protection: give the engineer a standing seat riding alongside the org's highest-visibility initiatives without separate negotiation each time.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Give a standing seat riding along top-visibility initiatives, no renegotiation

### 28. Attribute security disclosures to the engineer via public CVE credit

Make the engineer the disclosed author on public security-vulnerability disclosures (CVE credits), so recognition runs through a public registry, not a resume line.

- Fund one externally visible technical artifact under the engineer's own byline, such as a public write-up or filed patent, each year.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Fund one externally visible artifact under the engineer's byline every year

### 29. Give the engineer unilateral kill/greenlight authority over a project without consensus

Give the engineer authority to greenlight or kill an entire product line, since build cost no longer constrains what gets attempted.

- Give the engineer authority to kill a project outright, including one a founder or executive proposed, without needing consensus.
- Give the engineer unilateral authority to deprecate a legacy system, a decision normally gated by committee.
- Let the engineer decide unilaterally which live experiments get killed after data comes in, replacing a steering-committee review with individual judgment.

### 30. Designate the specific engineer as the public face/voice during incidents

Give the engineer the public voice on the status page and incident channel during outages, attaching a name to crisis communication.

- For the one named engineer, put their face and name on the company's external status page as the person customers can identify with the system.
- At ten thousand times headcount, replace individual designation with a standing rule: whoever owns a system by tenure automatically becomes its external incident spokesperson, no appointment needed.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Auto-assign incident-spokesperson role by tenure/ownership rule, no appointment

### 31. Overstaff relative to ticket volume to free protected build time

Staff the team slightly ahead of ticket volume so the tenured engineer gets protected time to build rather than only firefight.

### 32. Auto-route ownerless cross-team problems to the engineer by standing rule

Automatically route any cross-team failure with no clear owner to the senior engineer as default owner, so ambiguity supplies new situations on a schedule.

- As mycorrhizal fungal networks preferentially channel carbon to connected trees, route the org's hardest, most visible problems to senior engineers so internal reputation compounds independent of any employer's brand name.
- Route the hardest open bug anywhere in the customer base directly to the senior engineer, regardless of which team owns the code.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Route the hardest cross-team bug to the engineer regardless of ownership

### 33. Route unfiltered customer calls or feedback to the engineer and let them decide fix priority

Put the engineer directly on live customer calls, since the cost of reaching a real counterparty has collapsed, and let them decide what gets fixed.

- Route unfiltered prospective-customer feedback straight to the engineer, since discovery cost has crashed, and let them decide the fix priority.

### 34. Let engineer sign off on external technical/SLA claims to customers

Let the engineer sign off on external technical claims (SLAs, security posture) made to customers, since finding counterparties is cheap but being trusted to represent them is not.

### 35. Attach a visible dollar-impact metric to the engineer's name in reporting

Attach a visible dollar-impact business metric directly to the engineer's name in company-wide reporting.

- Mimic ant pheromone trail reinforcement, where repeated use strengthens a foraging path: continuously broadcast the engineer's technical wins through a visible internal signal chain so they stay the strongest-marked route others follow.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Continuously broadcast the engineer's wins through an internal signal channel

### 36. Assign a standing internal executive sponsor to publicly vouch for the engineer

Assign a fixed executive sponsor whose explicit job for two years is to vouch publicly for the engineer's growing scope.

### 37. Name the engineer on the customer contract as technical signatory or responsible architect

Get customer contracts to name the engineer by name as the responsible architect, so their name appears on external paper the same way a vendor's brand does.

- Assign the engineer as the named technical signatory on a contract with an external customer, so that customer's engineers deal with them directly, not a manager.

### 38. Attribute the engineer's assessment by name in diligence materials

Put the engineer's written assessment into every acquisition or partnership diligence memo, named and traceable in board materials.

- Give the engineer signing authority on technical due-diligence responses during a fundraising or acquisition conversation.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Give the engineer signing authority on due-diligence responses

### 39. Hand the senior engineer every acquisition/vendor diligence review

1	# The pipeline
2	
3	The operational detail behind Phases 1-4: which sub-agent runs each stage, what each writes, and
4	which script checks it. **Read this before generating anything** — you cannot run the steps
5	without it, and every stage after generation depends on the file the stage before it wrote.
6	
7	This is the same pipeline whichever way the skill was invoked. The `/ideas` command exists only
8	to make invocation reliable; it does not change what runs.
9	
10	Several rules below carry a short piece of evidence — a run that did the other thing. The full
11	narratives live in `docs/INCIDENTS.md` **in the repository**, which does not ship with the skill and
12	which you do not need: every rule here is complete as written. Read it when deciding whether a rule
13	can be relaxed, not when following one.
14	
15	Requires sub-agent dispatch, `python3` and a Bash tool. Those three fail differently and the
16	fallbacks are not interchangeable.
17	
18	**No sub-agent dispatch** — run the lenses as sequential passes in your own context, per
19	`SKILL.md` Phase 1. That fallback is written there and you must disclose taking it.
20	
21	**No Bash or no `python3`** — the scripts do not ship in the zip or the `.agents/` mirror either,
22	so this is the normal case on those install routes rather than an exotic one. The pipeline still
23	runs: every stage below is a thing a model does, and only the checks between them are executable.
24	What you lose is worth naming to the reader in one line, because these are the guarantees this
25	skill advertises:
26	
27	- **The integrity check** (`verify_pipeline.py`). Nothing proves `generated == presented +
28	  rejected`. Do the arithmetic yourself and state the three numbers; a count you did by hand is
29	  weaker evidence than a count a script refused to skip, and the reader should know which they got.
30	- **The generated report skeleton** (`build_report.py`). You assemble the report by hand, so the
31	  guarantee that every option reaches the page becomes an intention rather than a construction —
32	  and the depth fields for the leading options stop being enforced slots and become a template you
33	  have to remember. Work from the family list in rank order and do not summarise it.
34	- **The adjudicator agreement probe** (`shard_candidates.py`, `merge_relations.py`). No pairs are
35	  double-judged, so the run measures nothing about how stable its own grouping is. Say so rather
36	  than reporting a grouping as though its reliability were known.
37	
38	Sharding and merging themselves you can do in your own context; they cost context rather than
39	correctness. **Say in one line which of these you lost.** A run that quietly drops the checks and
40	describes itself in the same words as a checked run is the failure this whole pipeline exists to
41	prevent.
42	
43	## Step 0 — resolve `$CPS` before any other step
44	
45	Every script below is called as `python3 "$CPS/scripts/<name>.py"`. Resolve `CPS` once, first,
46	with the block below. Run it exactly as written and read the `CPS=` line it prints.
47	
48	**Why it is a search and not an edit.** The path you read this file at is a **file-tool** path.
49	The scripts are run by the **shell**. On some hosts those are different filesystem namespaces —
50	not different working directories, different mounts of the same content at different absolute
51	paths — and there is **no string that is correct for both**. On Cowork's host loop the file tools
52	report the plugin under the user's home directory while the shell sees it under
53	`/sessions/<session>/mnt/.remote-plugins/<plugin id>`. Stripping a known tail off the first
54	produces a path the shell cannot stat, and an upward walk from it searches a tree that is not
55	there — so both halves of the old instruction failed together, for one shared reason, and
56	produced "scripts not found" on a host where the scripts were present and working.
57	
58	That is a different problem from Step 0b's, and it has a different answer. Step 0b's run directory
59	is one place with **two spellings**, so each tool family is handed the spelling it accepts. The
60	plugin root is **two places**, so the shell has to find its own.
61	
62	```sh
63	# CPS-RESOLVER — executable as written; the test suite extracts and runs this block.
64	cps_resolve() {                    # $1 = the path you read THIS file at
65	  READ_AT="$1"
66	  SENTINEL="scripts/verify_pipeline.py"
67	  # The COMPLETE root list, overridable as one variable, ONE ROOT PER LINE. Not a default plus a hard-coded
68	  # tail: a search with roots the caller cannot control cannot be tested, because the fixture
69	  # cannot stop it reaching the real install and answering correctly for the wrong reason.
70	  #
71	  # ONE ROOT PER LINE, not space-separated. Desktop's local agent mode stages plugins under
72	  # "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude/local-agent-mode-sessions/<session>/<sub>/rpm/", and
73	  # a space-separated list word-splits "Application Support" into two roots that do not exist.
74	  # Measured on a machine with that shape: the old three roots returned ZERO hits while a
75	  # complete install sat under Application Support -- branch 1 happened to save it, and would not
76	  # have on a split host.
77	  ROOTS="${CPS_SEARCH_ROOTS:-$(printf '%s\n' /sessions "$HOME/.claude/plugins" "$HOME/.claude" "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude")}"
78	  CAND="${READ_AT%/skills/creative-problem-solving/references/pipeline.md}"
79	  PID=$(basename "$CAND")
80	
81	  # Branch 1 — the string edit, VERIFIED rather than trusted. Free, and guaranteed to be the
82	  # same install as the file you just read, which no other branch can promise.
83	  if [ -f "$CAND/$SENTINEL" ]; then
84	    CPS="$CAND"; echo "CPS=$CPS (branch 1: path as read)"; return 0
85	  fi
86	
87	  # Between the branches: if the shell CAN see the directory the file tools named, it can judge
88	  # this install directly, and searching elsewhere would be a mistake rather than a fallback.
89	  # A skills-only install (the zip, the .agents mirror, an older version that shipped skills/ and
90	  # nothing else) reaches this point legitimately, and the global search below would bind it to a
91	  # DIFFERENT version's scripts sitting elsewhere on the same disk — or refuse because two of them
92	  # are. Measured locally: reading pipeline.md from a cached 0.1.0 (skills/ only) refused with two
93	  # copies found, instead of taking the documented scriptless fallback written for exactly it.
94	  #
95	  # Gated on visibility, and that gate is load-bearing. On a split-namespace host $CAND is a path
96	  # from the OTHER filesystem: `[ -d "$CAND" ]` is false there not because the install is odd but
97	  # because the shell cannot see it. Measured on Cowork host loop — the file tools report the
98	  # plugin somewhere under the user's own home directory (deliberately not spelled out here: a
99	  # literal host path in this file becomes model-visible text and trips the runtime host-path
100	  # guard, which is how this very line was caught) while the shell has the same plugin under
101	  # /sessions/<id>/mnt/.remote-plugins/. If
102	  # this test ran unconditionally, every host-loop run would conclude "scriptless" and take the
103	  # degraded path, which is the exact silent downgrade this whole block exists to prevent.
104	  if [ -d "$CAND" ]; then
105	    if [ -d "$CAND/agents" ] || [ -d "$CAND/../agents" ]; then
106	      echo "REFUSING: $CAND is a plugin install — it has an agents/ directory — but carries no"
107	      echo "  $SENTINEL. Its scripts are missing. Another copy elsewhere on this disk is a"
108	      echo "  DIFFERENT version, and running its scripts against these instructions is the"
109	      echo "  version skew this step exists to prevent. Reinstall the plugin, or set CPS by hand."
110	      return 2
111	    fi
112	    echo "CPS= (branch 1b: visible install with no scripts/ and no agents/ — this is the zip, the"
113	    echo "  .agents/ mirror, or a skills-only version. They ship without scripts/ by design. Take"
114	    echo "  the SKILL.md Phase 1 fallback and say in one line which checks the run lost.)"
115	    return 1
116	  fi
117	
118	  # $CAND is not visible. That has TWO causes wanting different answers, and `[ -d ]` alone
119	  # cannot tell them apart: the path belongs to another filesystem, or it is simply wrong.
120	  # Decide it without ever stat-ing a path from the other side — the shell's own location and the
121	  # read path's shape are enough. Under Cowork's host loop the shell sits under /sessions/ and the
122	  # file tools report a host path that does not; under its VM loop BOTH are under /sessions/, so
123	  # a missing directory there really is missing.
124	  SPLIT=0
125	  case "$PWD" in /sessions/*) SPLIT=1 ;; esac
126	  case "$HOME" in /sessions/*) SPLIT=1 ;; esac
127	  case "$CAND" in /sessions/*) SPLIT=0 ;; esac
128	
129	  # Branch 0 — ask the shell, which is the only party whose answer is already in the shell's own
130	  # namespace. Claude Code puts <plugin root>/bin on the Bash tool's PATH, constructed for that
131	  # shell rather than inherited, so a bare `cps` is looked up by the shell itself and NOTHING
132	  # crosses the namespace boundary. On a split host that replaces the search below outright.
133	  #
134	  # DELIBERATELY BELOW BRANCH 1, AND GATED ON SPLIT. Branch 1 is the only branch that can promise
135	  # the scripts belong to the install whose instructions you are reading; a launcher promises a
136	  # working install, not THAT install. Run first, it silently preferred a marketplace copy over
137	  # the checkout the model was reading -- reproduced with two installs and a `cps` pointing at the
138	  # older one, which is the ordinary shape of a maintainer's own machine. Ordering it here costs
139	  # nothing: where branch 1 can answer, the search never runs anyway.
140	  #
141	  # The SPLIT gate is the same consistency: with shared namespaces a read path that does not
142	  # resolve is a WRONG path, and the single-hit case below refuses it rather than binding another
143	  # copy. A launcher must not quietly do what that refusal exists to prevent.
144	  #
145	  # Ov

1	---
2	name: creative-problem-solving
3	description: Runs a long pipeline that generates hundreds of options for an open-ended problem across many isolated angles, checks the ones it presents most prominently by search, and presents every option it generated rather than a pruned few. Use ONLY when the user explicitly asks for it: the /ideas command, naming this skill, or saying "use creative problem solving on this". Do NOT select it merely because a prompt asks for ideas, options, angles, approaches, a brainstorm or a rethink, or says the obvious answers are spent — those are ordinary requests and answering them directly is almost always right. The cost is the reason: a full run takes about forty minutes and returns a long document, so it must be the user's deliberate choice and not an inference from phrasing. Not for problems with one correct answer, or for executing an idea already chosen.
4	compatibility: Requires sub-agent dispatch, python3 and a Bash tool to run the full pipeline; without them it degrades to sequential passes in a single context and says so. Uses web search to verify options.
5	metadata:
6	  author: Yaniv Golan
7	  email: yaniv@golan.name
8	  version: 0.3.0
9	---
10	
11	# Creative problem solving
12	
13	Named creativity frameworks mostly don't work on their own — in head-to-head testing,
14	SCAMPER and similar scored no better than a plain prompt, and some scored worse. What has
15	evidence behind it is narrower — reaching past the answer you would give first, rather than
16	decorating a single sweep with headings. This pipeline does that by generating each pass blind
17	under its own constraint, and by asking for enough options that the obvious ones are spent
18	early.
19	
20	So this is an engine, not a menu: the classic methods survive only as **constraint lenses**
21	applied one at a time. *Structure that makes the next idea harder to reach for helps; structure
22	that decorates a single sweep produces longer output that scores better and isn't better.*
23	
24	## When not to use this
25	
26	Problems with one correct answer, debugging, executing an already-chosen idea, or anything where
27	the user wants a decision rather than options. A four-phase divergence engine on "which of these
28	two should I pick" is the same mistake in the opposite direction.
29	
30	## Reference files
31	
32	- `references/pipeline.md` — the operative stages: sub-agent per stage, the file each writes,
33	  the scripts that check them. **Required reading before Phase 1**, not optional depth.
34	- `references/report.md` — the whole of Phase 4. **Required before you write anything the user
35	  sees.**
36	- `references/pruning.md` — the Phase 3 steps. **Required before you prune.**
37	- `references/gotchas.md` — the failure modes this pipeline actually produces (framework theater,
38	  temperature, premature convergence and the rest), with what each one costs. Read it when
39	  something is going wrong, or once before your first run.
40	- `references/lenses.md` — longer worked prompts per lens, plus the demoted ones (SCAMPER, Six
41	  Thinking Hats) and why. **Optional**: the Phase 1 table carries both moves for every lens. Read
42	  it when a lens isn't landing, not as routine.
43	- `references/evidence.md` — what the research supports, and how strongly. Read if the user
44	  challenges the approach, or before skipping or changing a phase.
45	
46	**If this file appears to end early, it did — re-read it from disk before continuing.** A long
47	conversation truncates a skill body and leaves a marker where it cut; a phase named above being
48	simply absent means the same. This catches only the visible failure — a skill dropped from a
49	conversation entirely leaves no trace.
50	
51	`docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md` is for humans maintaining this and is **not** in the installed skill. Don't
52	read it at runtime.
53	
54	## Grounding
55	
56	Every run is grounded in two places.
57	
58	**Phase 0 retrieves what already exists** and hands that list to every generator as a
59	difference constraint — *your ideas must not be any of these*. This is what stops the pipeline
60	re-deriving the field's standard answers and calling them options.
61	
62	**Phase 3 checks by search the borrowed mechanism behind the lead option of each of the top 13 families.** Not every option: the lead, where it
63	rests on a claim about the outside world — how an organism works, what an institution does. If it
64	does not verify, cut it: a borrowed mechanism that isn't real is not an option, it is a fabrication
65	that reads as confident. **Variants nested under a lead are not checked**, and neither is the
66	judgement prose around them.
67	
68	**Options below the top 13 ship unverified and say so**, with an offer to verify any of them on
69	request. Checking a hundred-plus options is not affordable; naming which ones were checked is.
70	
71	Say roughly how long you will take, then go. Don't ask permission twice.
72	
73	---
74	
75	## Phase 0 — Sharpen the brief
76	
77	Cheap and the highest-leverage phase. Never skip it.
78	
79	**1. Find the function, not the form.** Restate the problem as the job to be done, stripped
80	of any implied solution. "Design a better pill bottle" → "ensure a person takes the right
81	dose at the right time." The form in the brief is the ceiling on the answer.
82	
83	**2. Build a banned-word list.** Ban the nouns naming a **shape of answer**; never the nouns
84	naming the **thing the answer is about**. Models echo the seed vocabulary, so taking the form
85	words away forces mechanism over label — while taking the subject words away leaves a pass
86	generating plausibly about nothing.
87	
88	Which is which is not a property of the word. Strike it from the sharpened brief and read the
89	brief back: if it no longer says what the problem is about, keep it. *"A better pill bottle"* →
90	ban **bottle, cap, dispenser**; keep **medication, dose, patient**. *"How to distribute this
91	document about X"* → ban **site, publish, newsletter, thread**; **X is not bannable**. A
92	generator has the brief and its lens and nothing else, so what the brief drops it cannot know.
93	Same rule as the retrieved neighbours below: a ban list is for shapes to avoid, never the subject.
94	
95	Then ban your own by the same test — **the sharpened brief anchors your passes harder than the
96	user's phrasing did**, because it *is* their prompt. Give each pass a different phrasing of the
97	same function; identical sentences give five copies of one starting point.
98	
99	**3. Write down the obvious answer — and set it aside.** Two lines on what a competent
100	generalist would say. This is the baseline every idea gets measured against, and naming it
101	early stops it reappearing later disguised as insight.
102	
103	**3b. Test the constraints the user ruled out.** When someone says "it's not the money",
104	"we've already tried X", or "that's not an option", they are reporting a conclusion, not a
105	fact. Spend one line asking whether it survives: *what would have to be true for the ruled-out
106	answer to still be the answer, and how would they check cheaply?*
107	
108	Accepting a ruled-out constraint isn't respecting the user, it's declining the part they
109	can't do themselves — they know what they've ruled out, and they're asking *because* it
110	didn't work. In testing a plain answer beat this skill by refusing "it's not the money":
111	benchmarks price year-one offers, so matched day-one comp decays annually. If the constraint
112	holds, say so in a line and move on. If it doesn't, that's often the answer.
113	
114	**4. Inject adversarial attributes.** Add 2-3 **surprising and negatively-valenced**
115	attributes to the working brief — this framing move produces larger novelty gains than any
116	choice of method. E.g. "…where the budget is falling", "…where the current best practice is
117	about to become illegal", "…where the cheapest input becomes the scarcest."
118	
119	**They describe the world, never anything of the asker's.** An attribute may say what is true
120	of the situation, the market, the technology, the regulation — conditions that would hold for
121	anyone facing this class of problem. It may **not** attribute a state, a number, an attitude or a
122	resource to the person asking, their team, their users, **their project, or anything they own or
123	run** — not as a claim, and not as a supposition either.
124	
125	The boundary, because it is easy to land on the wrong side of it: *"funding for work like this is
126	drying up"* is a pressure on the world. *"Your budget is falling"*, *"their CI is flaky"*, *"the
127	maintainers have no review time"* are invented facts about them, and naming a system rather than a
128	person does not help — a project's CI is theirs. Grammar does not help either: an option written
129	under a supposition does not carry the supposition with it, so by the time it reaches the reader it
130	is simply a statement about their situation.
131	
132	Record what you added, separately from what you were told, in `references/pipeline.md`
133	step 0c.
134	
135	Keep the sharpened brief as working state — it goes into the passes, not into the
136	answer. The exception: if the problem is ambiguous in a way that changes half the answers
137	("the verification step" could mean document KYC, an email link, or an SMS code), ask one
138	question before generating. That's not the same as asking permission to proceed — it's
139	cheaper than generating for the wrong reading. If you can't ask, pick the likeliest
140	reading and **say which one you picked** in the answer itself, with what changes under the
141	others. It is easy to forget once research has run, because the retrieved list makes the
142	chosen reading feel settled: in testing, the ungrounded run disclosed its reading and the
143	grounded one silently picked one.
144	
145	**One question, and only about meaning.** The bar is *the answers change*, not *it would be
146	useful to know*: scope, emphasis, target segment, detail level and output format all fail it.
147	An interview is not a divergence pass, and each question narrows the space before you've
148	explored it. When in doubt, generate and disclose — yo

1	# Constraint lenses
2	
3	Longer worked prompts for the nine lenses. **`SKILL.md`'s Phase 1 table is the operative
4	version** — it carries each lens's move and second move. Read this file when a lens isn't
5	landing, not as routine.
6	
7	## Contents
8	
9	- [Using a lens well](#using-a-lens-well)
10	- [The lenses](#the-lenses) — contradiction, first principles, inversion, constraint
11	  extremity, time-shift, analogical transfer, biomimicry, morphological, actor reversal
12	- [Demoted lenses](#demoted-lenses) — SCAMPER, Six Thinking Hats
13	- [Choosing lenses](#choosing-lenses-for-a-problem) — also condensed in the SKILL.md table
14	
15	---
16	
17	## Using a lens well
18	
19	The lens is a *constraint on the search*, not a template for the output — never fill in its
20	sections as headings. One lens per pass; two at once gives you the average of both.
21	
22	Every lens below has a **second move**, and it is reliably the one that gets skipped. The
23	Phase 1 table in `SKILL.md` carries both moves for all nine, so this file is for when a lens
24	isn't landing and you want the longer version.
25	
26	If a pass returns everything above p=0.3 it collapsed to the modal answer. Redo that one pass
27	with: *"every candidate was a high-probability answer — return 6 more from below p=0.1."*
28	Once only; twice produces noise dressed as novelty.
29	
30	## The lenses
31	
32	### Contradiction (TRIZ, stripped down)
33	
34	> Find the tradeoff that everyone working on this problem quietly accepts as a law of
35	> nature — "you can have X or Y, not both." State it explicitly. Then refuse it: generate
36	> approaches that get X and Y simultaneously, by changing what the system is made of,
37	> when the parts act, or where the boundary sits. If the tradeoff turns out to be a real
38	> physical or economic law, say so and instead attack whichever side of it is only
39	> conventionally true.
40	
41	Classical TRIZ resolution moves, useful as sub-prompts: segment the system into
42	independent parts; take the troublesome part out entirely; give different regions
43	different properties; introduce asymmetry; merge operations in time or space; make one
44	element do several jobs; nest one system inside another; do the required change in
45	advance; invert the direction of the action.
46	
47	Keep the contradiction-naming step — it forces an explicit statement of what's being
48	assumed, and it's why TRIZ survived the evidence review. Drop the 39×39 matrix ceremony.
49	
50	Best for: technical bottlenecks, structural constraints, "we can't do X because Y."
51	
52	### First principles
53	
54	> Strip the problem to what must be true regardless of how anyone currently solves it.
55	> List the current approach's assumptions one by one and mark each: physical law,
56	> economic law, regulation, or convention. Most will be convention. Discard everything
57	> that is convention and rebuild solutions using only the laws that remain. Do not check
58	> your rebuilt solution against how things are currently done.
59	
60	This is essentially task decomposition, the best-evidenced of all the framework-shaped
61	interventions. If you only have budget for one lens, use this one.
62	
63	Best for: mature industries, "that's just how it's done", suspected local minimum.
64	
65	### Inversion
66	
67	> Solve the opposite problem. If the goal is to increase X, generate the most effective
68	> ways to destroy X — be specific and mechanically plausible, not glib. Then invert each
69	> one into a defence or an opportunity. Separately: assume the goal has already been
70	> achieved and work backwards to what must have happened first.
71	
72	Denying the model the move it just made reliably pushes it into novel regions; inversion
73	is the cheapest version of that.
74	
75	Best for: when everything generated so far sounds the same; risk and defensive strategy.
76	
77	### Constraint extremity
78	
79	> Generate solutions under each of these separately, treating each as absolutely binding:
80	> (a) one hundredth of a normal budget for this kind of work; (b) it must work in one week;
81	> (c) no humans
82	> are involved at any step; (d) it must work for exactly one person; (e) it must work at
83	> ten thousand times the scale. Do not soften the constraint into something reasonable —
84	> if a constraint makes the current approach impossible, that's the point, and the
85	> replacement is the idea.
86	
87	Best for: capital-heavy or process-heavy incumbents, cost-structure problems.
88	
89	### Time-shift
90	
91	> Identify the single resource that a problem of this kind is usually scarce and expensive in,
92	> and that is getting cheaper fast. Assume it is free and unlimited. Generate what becomes
93	> possible, then work back to what is buildable on the current price curve. Separately:
94	> identify what becomes scarce *because* that resource became abundant — the new
95	> bottleneck is usually where the value moves.
96	
97	The second half is the valuable half and it's the one models skip. Push on it.
98	
99	Best for: anything touching fast-moving technology; strategy over a multi-year horizon.
100	
101	### Analogical transfer
102	
103	> Describe the problem as a pure function, with all domain vocabulary removed — e.g. "get
104	> a scarce resource to whoever values it most, without a central authority deciding."
105	> Find three fields that solved that same abstract function and are as far as possible
106	> from this domain — not adjacent industries. For each, describe the *mechanism* they
107	> used, then port the mechanism, not the surface features.
108	
109	Analogy mining is the best-evidenced *content* intervention available, and the strength is
110	entirely in the distance — adjacent domains produce adjacent ideas, and the measured
111	benefit grows with semantic distance. Push hard on it; treat a comfortable analogy as a
112	failed one.
113	
114	Best for: when you want structurally novel answers rather than better versions.
115	
116	### Biomimicry
117	
118	> State the function biologically: "how does nature move a fluid without a pump?", "how
119	> does nature defend without armour?" Identify organisms or ecosystems that solve it.
120	> For each you must give BOTH the organism AND the mechanism — the actual physical or
121	> chemical process, at a level someone could look up and check. Then abstract the
122	> principle away from the biology and apply it.
123	
124	Domains worth sweeping: structural (spider silk, bone remodelling, coral, nacre);
125	chemical (photosynthesis, enzyme catalysis, bioluminescence); behavioural (swarm
126	intelligence, symbiosis, quorum sensing, migration); ecological (nutrient cycling,
127	succession, redundancy, decomposition).
128	
129	**Grounding is mandatory.** An organism name with a hand-waved mechanism is the standard
130	failure mode of AI biomimicry — confident and wrong. Search verifies the borrowed mechanism behind
131	the lead option of each of the top 13 families; if it doesn't verify, cut it. A biomimicry option that
132	is a nested variant, or that falls below the top 13, ships unverified — and that label matters more
133	here than anywhere else.
134	
135	The same rule covers the analogical-transfer lens above and any idea resting on a claim
136	about how a real system works. A misremembered historical example carries the same risk as
137	an invented organism and reads just as confident. Phase 3 step 4 enforces this.
138	
139	Best for: efficiency, resilience, self-organisation, materials, distributed systems.
140	
141	### Morphological
142	
143	> List the 4-6 independent dimensions on which any solution must take a position (not
144	> features — dimensions, e.g. "who pays", "when value is delivered", "what is
145	> standardised"). For each, list 3-5 genuinely different options including at least one
146	> that no current player uses. Then — and this is the actual work — go through
147	> combinations and eliminate every pair of options that are mutually contradictory or
148	> jointly impossible. Report only the surviving combinations that are both internally
149	> consistent and unlike anything on the current market.
150	
151	**The pruning is the method.** Exhaustive enumeration collapses under combinatorial
152	explosion, and a model generates the grid so cheaply that it makes the volume problem
153	worse. A morphological pass without the cross-consistency prune is a machine for producing
154	filler. Short on budget? Skip this lens entirely rather than run it without the prune.
155	
156	Best for: business models, experimental design, many independent variables.
157	
158	### Actor reversal
159	
160	> List every actor in the system and what each currently gives and gets. Then
161	> systematically swap roles: the customer becomes the supplier, the regulator becomes the
162	> customer, the product becomes the distribution channel, the competitor becomes the
163	> infrastructure. For each swap that isn't absurd, describe what the business or system
164	> looks like from the other side.
165	
166	Best for: business-model problems, marketplaces, platform strategy, incumbent disruption.
167	
168	---
169	
170	## Demoted lenses
171	
172	Both are in wide use and neither survived the evidence review as a divergence tool. Kept
173	with narrowed scope rather than deleted, because each has one job it does well. Reasons in
174	`evidence.md`.
175	
176	### SCAMPER — iteration only, never a blank page
177	
178	Substitute / Combine / Adapt / Modify / Put to another use / Eliminate / Reverse.
179	
180	It's a checklist for transforming something that already exists, so it inherits that
181	thing's frame — which is why it didn't improve novelty in testing. Use it when the user has
182	a concrete artefact, process or product they want variations on; never to open a problem.
183	Eliminate and Reverse carry the weight; Modify reliably produces filler.
184	
185	### Six Thinking Hats — convergence only
186	
187	White facts / Red emotions / Black caution / Yellow optimism / Green creativity /
188	Blue process.
189	
190	The Green hat adds nothing a proper divergence phase doesn't do better. The Black hat is a

1	# Phase 4 — writing the report
2	
3	The whole of Phase 4: what the reader gets, the shape of an option, what happens when the answer
4	becomes a document, and the honesty rule. `SKILL.md` carries the one-paragraph version and sends
5	you here.
6	
7	**This is required reading before you write anything the user sees.** It is a reference rather than
8	part of the skill body for one reason: the skill body is truncated at a fixed length in a long
9	conversation, and Phase 4 sat past that cut — so the phase that produces the answer was the part
10	most likely to be missing when it was needed. Here it is read on demand and arrives whole.
11	
12	**One consequence to know.** A reference read into a long conversation can be compacted away like
13	any other content, and unlike a truncated skill body it leaves no marker saying so. If you are
14	writing the report and cannot recall the option shape or the honesty rule, read this file again
15	rather than reconstructing them.
16	
17	---
18	
19	Output in chat unless the user asks for a file.
20	
21	**Phases 0-3 are working state, not deliverable.** The user gets the ideas and the
22	judgement — not the brief you sharpened, not the lens names, not the cluster analysis.
23	Showing your process is the single easiest way to triple the word
24	count without adding information. In testing, skill responses ran 2-3× the length of a
25	plain answer and roughly half of that was apparatus.
26	
27	**If the cause of the problem isn't known, diagnosis comes first.** When the user reports a
28	symptom — a number that moved, something that stopped working — open with the candidate
29	causes and the cheapest way to tell them apart, *then* the options. If the reader has to
30	know which cause is live before any of your ideas apply, they need that first. Keep it to
31	about three lines: this is a signpost, not a section, and on a light question it will eat a
32	third of your budget if you let it.
33	
34	The most-repeated failure here, and it never feels like padding — each clause earns its
35	place and the paragraph still lands at triple budget. The tell: a diagnosis that lists its
36	candidate causes *and* argues for each. Name them, give the test, stop. (Observed: 157 words.)
37	
38	```
39	[If a reading was chosen for an ambiguous problem: one line naming it.]
40	[If cause is unknown: 2-4 candidate causes + the cheapest test to tell them apart. ~3 lines.]
41	[HARD CEILING on those two together: 4 lines, ~100 words. They often overlap — the reading
42	 you picked is frequently one of the candidate causes — and you may merge them into one
43	 short paragraph, but merging buys no extra length. Then stop and start the first option.]
44	
45	### [Idea name]
46	[2-3 sentences: the mechanism first, then what it produces.]
47	- What has to be true: [the load-bearing assumption]
48	- Failure mode / cost: [one line]
49	- Who runs it: [required whenever it needs people or a mandate the asker doesn't have]
50	
51	[…several of these, in the rank order the pipeline produced — see `references/pipeline.md`
52	step 7, which ranks by whether an option would survive vetting…]
53	
54	**Checked and failed:** [only options a search refuted, each with its source]
55	**What I'd look at first, and what would change that:** [your actual read + 1-2 things
56	the user knows and you don't]
57	```
58	
59	**Every option you generated appears in the answer.** Options proposing the same core
60	intervention are grouped into a family and shown together, the strongest leading and the rest
61	as one-line variants naming what differs. A mechanism four passes reached gets one place, not
62	four — but all four stay visible. Nothing is dropped for being similar to something else: a
63	wrong merge is unrecoverable, since the reader never learns the option existed, while a wrong
64	grouping costs them a line of reading.
65	
66	Only two things leave the list. An option whose own description concedes it does not answer the
67	question asked, and a borrowed mechanism that a search refuted — and the second is reported as
68	checked-and-failed, with the source, rather than deleted quietly.
69	
70	**Depth is what scales with the question, not count.** A light question gets the same complete
71	list with two bullets per option and one line of closing read; a strategic one gets three
72	bullets, a ranking and a fuller read. Keep each option to about four lines of prose: word
73	counts are a poor target because you cannot reliably count your own words, so a word budget
74	produces confident non-compliance.
75	
76	**Always end with a point of view.** On a light question that's one line, not a section — an
77	answer that lists options and declines to say which you'd pick has handed the work back.
78	
79	The raised ceilings are a **reallocation, not an expansion**. The budget comes from the cut
80	list, which shrinks as fewer ideas are cut. Options past the first four or five carry their
81	mechanism and a one-line risk and nothing else — a compact entry the reader can evaluate in a
82	few seconds. An option worth one line is worth more than an option that isn't there; an option
83	padded to four lines to look like the others is the failure above, wearing a new hat.
84	
85	**Present only live options.** This is narrower than it sounds, and it does not conflict with
86	Phase 3 step 3. That step says an option needing people the asker doesn't have is still worth
87	presenting *with that named* — "you'd need to hire someone who has run this" is useful.
88	What leaves the list is an option whose own description concedes it isn't the thing the user
89	asked for: "that's a different firm", "you'd now be an insurance business". The test is not
90	"is this hard to staff" but "does this still answer the question asked." Say so in a line
91	rather than deleting it silently.
92	
93	**And the inverse, which matters more.** Everything mechanically distinct that *does* answer the
94	question ships as an option. Duplicates are grouped, not dropped, and nothing leaves for being
95	an idea you suspect the reader will reject. Readers who asked for options are doing the rejecting; that is
96	what the failure-mode line is for. A promising option you buried is invisible to them, and
97	invisible is the one outcome they cannot recover from. When you are unsure whether something
98	survives, present it in compact form rather than cutting it.
99	
100	**Ordering and judgement are different jobs, and they will disagree.** The order is the
101	pipeline's: families arrive ranked by whether they would survive vetting (`references/pipeline.md`
102	step 7). What stops the safe idea burying the interesting ones is not the order but the rule that
103	nothing is cut — a strange option is never ranked out of existence, only ranked. Then say what
104	you'd actually look at first in the closing read, often not the top-ranked one. That divergence is
105	information, not an inconsistency: say both. And don't promise a ranking you don't give.
106	
107	Lead with the mechanism, not the benefit — a benefit-first idea is indistinguishable from
108	a slogan.
109	
110	The template is a **floor, not a form**. If an idea has nothing to say under a line, drop
111	the line. Three things that look like content and aren't:
112	
113	- *"Why it's not the obvious answer"* under every idea — you're arguing with a baseline the
114	  reader can't see. State the obvious answer once at the top if it's genuinely useful, or
115	  not at all.
116	- *The sharpened brief* as a section — it reads as jargon restatement of what they just
117	  told you.
118	### When the answer becomes a document
119	
120	Often the run ends in a file — a memo, a brief, a deck — asked for after the report. That
121	composition is a fresh generation pass with none of Phase 3's constraints attached, and it is
122	where a pruned pipeline grows back: hedged options harden into committed policy, *what has to be
123	true* and *who runs it* quietly drop out, and specificity the pipeline never produced gets
124	invented to fill a section out.
125	
126	- **Every number, threshold and named policy in the document must trace to pipeline output or
127	  to something the user gave you.** What traces to neither is invented — cut it, or write it as
128	  the open choice it is. A threshold that arrived only because the section needed one reads as
129	  authoritative precisely because nothing in the run ever argued for it.
130	- **Black-hat the document, not the pool.** The contradictions that matter are between sections
131	  written separately that were never adjacent until now — at Phase 3 they did not exist yet.
132	
133	### The honesty rule
134	
135	Treat **diversity as measurable, novelty as a hypothesis, feasibility as the user's
136	decision.** (Diversity is measured in the repo's eval lane, never in the answer.) This is
137	calibration, not modesty: model novelty judgements diverge from expert
138	judgement even when the reasoning looks sound, experts disagree with each other on
139	feasibility, and pre-execution novelty ratings have been shown to reverse once someone
140	actually builds the thing.
141	
142	So never write "this is a novel idea." Write "I did not find prior art for this — here's
143	where I looked, and here's who would already be doing it if it were obvious." The second
144	is falsifiable; the first isn't.
145	
146	**And never describe process that did not happen.** Don't say you ran passes you didn't run,
147	searched what you didn't search, or checked what you didn't check. This is the same rule as
148	above pointed at yourself, and it is the one failure this pipeline cannot survive: every
149	other claim it makes is auditable against the answer, but a process claim is only auditable
150	against the record, so the reader has no defence. If a mode was unavailable, say which and
151	move on — a named downgrade costs one line and keeps everything else worth believing.
152	
153	**Without web access:** open with *"No web access in this environment — the
154	outside claims below are unverified and stated as principles rather than citations."* Then do
155	exactly that — Phase 3 step 4's last bullet says how, and it cuts nothing for failing a check
156	that cou
