1	{"lens": "morphological", "pool": 8, "items": [
2	{"id": "p8-001", "text": "Give the engineer sole sign-off authority over one production system's architecture for a full year, with no committee override, recorded in a signed charter."},
3	{"id": "p8-002", "text": "Assign the engineer as the named technical signatory on a contract with an external customer, so that customer's engineers deal with them directly, not a manager."},
4	{"id": "p8-003", "text": "Put the engineer on a rotating seat on an external standards body or industry working group as the employer's sole delegate, unsupervised."},
5	{"id": "p8-004", "text": "Structure one bet per year where the engineer's own bonus, not the company's budget, is the collateral that's forfeited if the system fails."},
6	{"id": "p8-005", "text": "Let the engineer negotiate and own a vendor or supplier relationship end-to-end, including the commercial terms, not just the technical interface."},
7	{"id": "p8-006", "text": "Commit to a single irreversible launch decision (no rollback plan funded) and put the engineer's name on the public postmortem regardless of outcome."},
8	{"id": "p8-007", "text": "Grant the engineer a real, if small, revenue-share stake in one external deal they architect, paid out over years even after they leave."},
9	{"id": "p8-008", "text": "Set up a standing mandate with no end date and no re-approval cycle: the engineer owns the domain until they explicitly hand it off."},
10	{"id": "p8-009", "text": "Have the engineer publish the incident postmortem for a major outage under their own byline on a public engineering blog with no editorial review."},
11	{"id": "p8-010", "text": "Route one customer's escalation calls directly to the engineer with no support-tier filter, making their judgment the last word before the customer relationship."},
12	{"id": "p8-011", "text": "Build a structured consulting seat: after departure, the ex-engineer is contractually the first call for any question about the system they owned, paid hourly."},
13	{"id": "p8-012", "text": "Let the engineer choose and manage a small discretionary budget to hire a contractor or buy a tool for their bet, with no approval chain."},
14	{"id": "p8-013", "text": "Make the engineer the sole author of record on a patent or technical filing tied to the system, with their name preserved even after they leave."},
15	{"id": "p8-014", "text": "Pair the engineer with an external counterparty (a partner company's engineer) on a joint deliverable that both employers' names sit on publicly."},
16	{"id": "p8-015", "text": "Give the engineer authority to kill a project outright, including one a founder or executive proposed, without needing consensus."},
17	{"id": "p8-016", "text": "Structure the unit of work as a single multi-quarter bet with no intermediate checkpoints, judged only on the final external outcome."},
18	{"id": "p8-017", "text": "Let the engineer's decisions be reviewable only by an external, named panel of practitioners from other companies, bypassing the internal reporting chain."},
19	{"id": "p8-018", "text": "Attach a noncompete-free but named-successor clause: the engineer trains no one, and the system stays visibly attributed to them in documentation indefinitely."},
20	{"id": "p8-019", "text": "Have the engineer own the risk model directly: they set the acceptable failure rate for their system and answer for it to the board, not their manager."},
21	{"id": "p8-020", "text": "Create a joint venture-style unit where the engineer and an external investor or partner co-own the outcome, sharing both upside and downside contractually."},
22	{"id": "p8-021", "text": "Assign the engineer a single named external client account that persists across projects, so their standing with that client outlasts any internal reorg."},
23	{"id": "p8-022", "text": "Make the unit of work an open bug bounty or public challenge that the engineer designs and judges, with their name attached as the arbiter."},
24	{"id": "p8-023", "text": "Let the engineer set and publish the technical roadmap for a product line externally (to customers or press) before it is finalized internally."},
25	{"id": "p8-024", "text": "Give the engineer discretion to reject the employer's own executive's technical request in writing, with that written rejection kept as the system's decision record."},
26	{"id": "p8-025", "text": "Structure the exit relationship as a paid handoff obligation: the departing engineer is contractually paid to write the definitive external-facing design document before leaving."},
27	{"id": "p8-026", "text": "Let the engineer co-sign the annual reliability or security disclosure filed with a regulator or auditor, putting their name on a document with legal weight."},
28	{"id": "p8-027", "text": "Have the engineer own a shared risk pool with the employer where losses on their bet are split contractually 50/50, unlike standard blameless postmortems."},
29	{"id": "p8-028", "text": "Give the engineer the right to represent the company at a customer's board meeting when a technical bet is being evaluated, in place of an executive."},
30	{"id": "p8-029", "text": "Make the unit of work a fixed irreversible external commitment (a published SLA to a named client) the engineer alone sets and is held to."},
31	{"id": "p8-030", "text": "Grant the engineer ownership of a named external credential the company sponsors them into (e.g., a seat on an accreditation board) that follows them after they leave."}
32	]}

2	{"id": "p9-001", "text": "Treat the engineer as a client: let them choose which incoming contracts the firm takes on, vetoing work that doesn't match the scope they want."},
3	{"id": "p9-002", "text": "Have the employer bid for the engineer's time against a running list of the engineer's outside offers, matching scope and authority contract by contract, not once a year."},
4	{"id": "p9-003", "text": "Route the engineer's internal tools and writeups through a larger company's public engineering blog or conference slot as a guest contributor, using the rival as a distribution channel rather than a destination."},
5	{"id": "p9-004", "text": "Have the employer pitch recruiters at the engineer's target companies directly, briefing them on the engineer's decision scope so they carry an accurate, upgraded story onward."},
6	{"id": "p9-005", "text": "Put the engineer in the room with paying customers as the accountable decision-maker on scope and tradeoffs, so the customer directs the roadmap the way a manager would."},
7	{"id": "p9-006", "text": "Run the exit conversation as a sales negotiation: before any departure, offer a standing paid advisory contract the engineer can decline or take, priced like a client deal."},
8	{"id": "p9-007", "text": "Have the newest junior engineers submit written evaluations of the senior engineer's architecture calls, which get compiled into an external-facing record of decisions made and their outcomes."},
9	{"id": "p9-008", "text": "Give the engineer a standing slot presenting technical risk directly to the board and investors, bypassing the management layer that normally filters that information upward."},
10	{"id": "p9-009", "text": "Broker a paid loan-out arrangement where a larger company pays for a fixed number of the engineer's days per quarter to solve one of its hard problems, while employment stays put."},
11	{"id": "p9-010", "text": "Convene a panel of engineers from other companies to formally review this engineer's system designs on a schedule, producing an external record of judgment exercised."},
12	{"id": "p9-011", "text": "Have the employer act as booking agent for the engineer's outside speaking and advisory work, negotiating terms and taking a cut like a talent agency would."},
13	{"id": "p9-012", "text": "Get customer contracts to name the engineer by name as the responsible architect, so their name appears on external paper the same way a vendor's brand does."},
14	{"id": "p9-013", "text": "Invite senior engineers from larger companies to sign off formally on this engineer's system design as an outside certifier, producing a credential the small employer couldn't mint alone."},
15	{"id": "p9-014", "text": "Give the engineer a discretionary budget to directly hire and manage contractors for their own initiatives, making them a buyer of labour rather than only a seller of it."},
16	{"id": "p9-015", "text": "License production traffic or workload data from a larger company so the engineer solves problems at that company's scale without needing to work there."},
17	{"id": "p9-016", "text": "Give the engineer a quarterly slot presenting technical strategy directly to investors on the call, in place of or alongside the CEO."},
18	{"id": "p9-017", "text": "Make the engineer a required signatory on customer contracts above a size threshold, giving them formal veto power over deals rather than advisory input."},
19	{"id": "p9-018", "text": "Give the engineer direct headcount authority to hire their own reports without going through a manager, making them the effective owner of a hiring line."},
20	{"id": "p9-019", "text": "Win contracts too large to deliver alone and subcontract pieces of them to larger companies, with this engineer named as the prime contractor's technical lead."},
21	{"id": "p9-020", "text": "Tie the engineer's compensation to a specific customer account's renewal and expansion, making them financially exposed like an owner rather than a delivery resource."},
22	{"id": "p9-021", "text": "Pay recruiters and headhunters a bounty not to place the engineer elsewhere but to route interesting outside technical problems and client leads to them instead."},
23	{"id": "p9-022", "text": "Have the engineer personally warrant production reliability to customers in writing, like a professional engineer's stamp, carrying named liability the employer doesn't absorb."},
24	{"id": "p9-023", "text": "Give the engineer a board observer seat, sitting in the room where budget and roadmap decisions actually get made rather than hearing them relayed."},
25	{"id": "p9-024", "text": "When a larger company makes an offer, have the employer sit at the table as the engineer's negotiating advisor rather than as the party being left."},
26	{"id": "p9-025", "text": "Let the engineer negotiate directly with the largest customer's engineering leadership on technical scope, cutting out the account manager as intermediary."},
27	{"id": "p9-026", "text": "Have the engineer chair a cross-company technical working group setting a shared standard, representing the employer's interests the way a much larger firm's delegate would."},
28	{"id": "p9-027", "text": "Publish the engineer's post-incident reviews and architecture decisions under their own byline to customers and prospects, the way a larger firm would use its brand name."},
29	{"id": "p9-028", "text": "Let the engineer set the price and scope of the employer's next hard technical engagement with a customer, acting as the internal seller rather than the delivery staff."},
30	{"id": "p9-029", "text": "Have the engineer interview and select the employer's next major customer or partner, reversing the usual flow where customers select vendors."},
31	{"id": "p9-030", "text": "Route unsolicited recruiter outreach to the engineer through the employer first, letting the engineer instruct the employer on which outside conversations to help arrange."}
32	]}

def pack(clusters, cap):
    """First-fit-decreasing over WHOLE clusters, so no cluster is split across two dispatches.

    A cluster larger than the cap becomes a task larger than the cap. Keeping the cluster whole is
    the right call -- splitting one across two dispatches means neither can see it, and deciding
    whether it holds more than one mechanism is the job -- but the resulting task is over budget and
    the caller must say so rather than let a silent breach through.
    """
    tasks = []
    for c in sorted(clusters, key=lambda x: (-len(x), x[0])):
        for t in tasks:
            if sum(len(x) for x in t) + len(c) <= cap: t.append(c); break
        else: tasks.append([c])
    return tasks


def main(wd, max_task, split_over):
    pools = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(wd, "pool-*.json")))
    if not pools: die(f"no pool-*.json in {wd}")
    ids, text = [], {}
    for p in pools:
        for it in (load(p, "items") or []):
            ids.append(it["id"]); text[it["id"]] = it.get("text", "")
    if not ids: die("the pools carry no options")

    rel = {}
    for e in load(os.path.join(wd, "relations.json"), "relations"):
        rel[frozenset((e["a"], e["b"]))] = relation_of(e, "relations.json")

    clusters = []
    for comp in positive_components(ids, rel):
        clusters += relocate(agglomerate(comp, rel), rel)
    placed = [m for c in clusters for m in c]
    if sorted(placed) != sorted(ids):
        die(f"partition lost or duplicated options: {len(placed)} placed against {len(ids)} generated")

    leads, viol, proven = choose_leads(clusters, rel)
    # A PROVEN-INFEASIBLE PINCH IS MERGED, NOT REFUSED.
    #
    # Intransitivity makes this reachable by construction, not by accident: 12-25% of fully judged
    # triples have two pairs joining and the third separating, so a cluster pair whose every lead
    # choice collides is a shape the verdicts themselves produce. The first live run to hit it was
    # told "this is a bug in the partition, not something the grouper can fix" -- which named no
    # action, was not true (the cross verdicts were implementation_variant and distinct, not all
    # the same intervention), and cost about eleven minutes of improvised repair.
    #
    # Merging follows the same doctrine merge_families.py already applies: when nothing can
    # separate two groups' leads, they are one group, and merging contradicts no verdict. Only a
    # COMPLETED search licenses it.
    merged_pinch = 0
    while viol and proven:
        i, j = min(((a, b) for a, b in viol), key=lambda p: (clusters[p[0]][0], clusters[p[1]][0]))
        clusters[i] = sorted(clusters[i] + clusters[j])
        clusters.pop(j)
        merged_pinch += 1
        leads, viol, proven = choose_leads(clusters, rel)
    if viol:
        die(f"the search for distinct cluster leads ran out of budget with {len(viol)} pair(s) "
            f"still colliding, so whether an assignment exists is UNKNOWN rather than impossible. "
            f"Re-run plan_groups.py with --lead-budget above {LEAD_NODES}. If it still exhausts, the "
            f"joinable graph is denser than this stage can settle: re-run with --max-task smaller "
            f"so the clusters it must separate are smaller.")

    order = sorted(range(len(clusters)), key=lambda i: (-len(clusters[i]), clusters[i][0]))
    out = [{"cid": f"c{n+1:03d}", "members": clusters[i], "lead": leads[i],
            "split_candidate": len(clusters[i]) > split_over} for n, i in enumerate(order)]
    json.dump({"clusters": out}, open(os.path.join(wd, "clusters.json"), "w", encoding="utf-8"),
              separators=(",", ":"))

    by_cid = {c["cid"]: c for c in out}
    packed = pack([c["members"] for c in out], max_task)
    for k, group in enumerate(packed, 1):
        cids = [next(c["cid"] for c in out if c["members"] == g) for g in group]
        json.dump({"task": k, "clusters": [
            {"cid": cid, "lead": by_cid[cid]["lead"],
             "split_candidate": by_cid[cid]["split_candidate"],
             "options": [{"id": m, "text": text[m]} for m in by_cid[cid]["members"]]}
            for cid in cids]},
            open(os.path.join(wd, f"group-task-{k}.json"), "w", encoding="utf-8"),
            indent=1)

    sizes = sorted((len(c["members"]) for c in out), reverse=True)
    singles = sum(1 for s in sizes if s == 1)
    big = [c for c in out if c["split_candidate"]]
    over = [t for t in packed if sum(len(x) for x in t) > max_task]
    if over:
        worst = max(sum(len(x) for x in t) for t in over)
        print(f"WARN: {len(over)} grouping task(s) exceed the {max_task}-option budget, the largest "
              f"at {worst}. A single cluster larger than the budget cannot be split across "
              f"dispatches without hiding it from both, so it ships whole — but it is the task most "
              f"likely to be slow, and the one whose split matters most. Check its result first.")
    print(f"{len(ids)} options -> {len(out)} clusters "
          f"(largest {sizes[0]}, {singles} single-member, {100*singles/len(out):.0f}%); "
          f"{len(packed)} grouping task(s), largest {max(sum(len(x) for x in t) for t in packed)} options; "
          f"{len(big)} cluster(s) over {split_over} members to check for themes")
    # Say where the bytes actually went, resolved. A caller cannot get this from a Write
    # result -- that echoes the path it was given -- and the shell's working directory is not
    # the file tools'. On a surface where those differ, a relative path in the summary names
    # a place the reader may not be able to reach, and the run looks identical either way.
    print(f"  wrote to {os.path.abspath(wd)}")

def choose_leads(clusters, rel, rounds=12):
    """Pick each cluster's lead so that no two leads were adjudicated as the same intervention.

    verify_pipeline refuses a run where two families lead with a `duplicate` or
    `implementation_variant` pair, because the report prints leads in full and the reader is then
    shown one move twice under two headings. The lead is otherwise the model's call -- this only
    overrides where the gate would fail, which on recorded runs is 0-4 clusters, i.e. at most 12% of
    the multi-member ones.
    """
    order = sorted(range(len(clusters)), key=lambda i: (-len(clusters[i]), clusters[i][0]))
    lead = {i: clusters[i][0] for i in range(len(clusters))}
    for i in order:
        lead[i] = min(clusters[i], key=lambda m: (
            sum(1 for j, l in lead.items() if j != i and rel.get(frozenset((m, l))) in JOINING), m))
    for _ in range(rounds):
        viol = [(i, j) for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(len(clusters)), 2)
                if rel.get(frozenset((lead[i], lead[j]))) in JOINING]
        if not viol: break
        moved = False
        for i in sorted({x for pair in viol for x in pair},
                        key=lambda i: (len(clusters[i]), clusters[i][0])):
            cur = sum(1 for j, l in lead.items()
                      if j != i and rel.get(frozenset((lead[i], l))) in JOINING)
            cand = min(clusters[i], key=lambda m: (
                sum(1 for j, l in lead.items() if j != i and rel.get(frozenset((m, l))) in JOINING), m))
            new = sum(1 for j, l in lead.items() if j != i and rel.get(frozenset((cand, l))) in JOINING)
            if new < cur: lead[i] = cand; moved = True
        if not moved: break

    # Greedy can stall where a complete search succeeds: a cluster keeps a lead that only collides
    # because of a choice made elsewhere, and no single move improves things. When that happens,
    # re-solve the whole assignment as a constraint problem rather than only the clusters currently
    # in a collision -- the freeing move is often in a cluster that looks fine.
    #
    # Ordered by fewest candidates first so the tight clusters fail early, and capped: past the
    # budget the greedy answer stands and step 9 reports the collision rather than the run hanging.
    proven = True
    if viol:
        NODES = LEAD_NODES
        cand = {i: sorted(clusters[i]) for i in range(len(clusters))}
        order2 = sorted(range(len(clusters)), key=lambda i: (len(cand[i]), clusters[i][0]))
        budget = [NODES]
        sol = {}

        def place(k):
            if budget[0] <= 0: return False
            if k == len(order2): return True
            i = order2[k]
            for m in cand[i]:
                budget[0] -= 1
                if budget[0] <= 0: return False
                if any(rel.get(frozenset((m, sol[j]))) in JOINING for j in sol): continue
                sol[i] = m
                if place(k + 1): return True
                del sol[i]
            return False

        if place(0):
            lead = dict(sol)
            viol = [(i, j) for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(len(clusters)), 2)
                    if rel.get(frozenset((lead[i], lead[j]))) in JOINING]
        else:
            # Budget left means the tree was exhausted: no assignment EXISTS. Budget gone means
            # the search was cut off and the answer is UNKNOWN. The caller must not treat these
            # alike -- one licenses merging clusters, the other licenses only asking for more
            # budget, and merging on "unknown" fuses clusters a longer search would have kept
            # apart.
            proven = budget[0] > 0

    return [lead[i] for i in range(len(clusters))], viol, proven

5	{"id": "p1-004", "text": "Publish the engineer's name, not the company's, as author on every severity-1 postmortem the company releases publicly."},
6	{"id": "p1-005", "text": "Give the engineer the company's sole delegate seat on an industry standards or working group, attached permanently to their name."},
7	{"id": "p1-006", "text": "Let the engineer negotiate and sign the technical clauses of vendor and customer contracts directly, without a management sign-off step."},
8	{"id": "p1-007", "text": "Embed the engineer inside a customer's engineering team for a fixed stretch each year, working the customer's system instead of yours."},
9	{"id": "p1-008", "text": "Assign every acquisition or vendor technical due-diligence review to the senior engineer, handing them someone else's decade of undocumented decisions to judge."},
10	{"id": "p1-009", "text": "Put the engineer on call for a partner or vendor's production system under a formal support agreement, so unfamiliar failures keep arriving on schedule."},
11	{"id": "p1-010", "text": "Have the engineer co-author, under joint attribution, the postmortem for any customer outage where your product was implicated."},
12	{"id": "p1-011", "text": "Give the engineer signing authority over infrastructure and vendor spend above a set threshold, independent of how many people report to them."},
13	{"id": "p1-012", "text": "Make the engineer the named technical reference prospective customers call before signing, attaching their voice directly to sales credibility."},
14	{"id": "p1-013", "text": "Route the hardest open bug anywhere in the customer base directly to the senior engineer, regardless of which team owns the code."},
15	{"id": "p1-014", "text": "Loan the engineer to a portfolio company or partner facing an active crisis for a fixed number of weeks each year."},
16	{"id": "p1-015", "text": "Publish the engineer's architecture reviews externally under a personally verified byline, separate from the company's own brand or blog."},
17	{"id": "p1-016", "text": "Give the engineer veto power over architecture decisions across every team in the company, not just their own, widening judgment scope instead of org size."},
18	{"id": "p1-017", "text": "Have the engineer run the post-incident review for every team's incidents company-wide, so novelty comes from breadth of exposure rather than company scale."},
19	{"id": "p1-018", "text": "Insert the engineer into quarterly board risk reporting so they present technical risk directly to the board, without a VP in between."},
20	{"id": "p1-019", "text": "Assign the one system nobody fully understands — legacy, acquired, undocumented — exclusively to the engineer, importing complexity instead of manufacturing traffic scale."},
21	{"id": "p1-020", "text": "Let the engineer negotiate SLA terms directly with the largest customer, bypassing account management entirely."},
22	{"id": "p1-021", "text": "Make the engineer the standing point of escalation for any subpoena, law-enforcement request, or compliance demand touching engineering systems."},
23	{"id": "p1-022", "text": "Give the engineer the public voice on the status page and incident channel during outages, attaching a name to crisis communication."},
24	{"id": "p1-023", "text": "Second the engineer into a customer's incident-command structure by name during that customer's worst outages, invited as an outside expert."},
25	{"id": "p1-024", "text": "Have the engineer co-sign the technical risk section of the company's insurance or audit filings alongside the CTO."},
26	{"id": "p1-025", "text": "Give the engineer discretion to hire and directly manage outside contractors for fixed stretches, generating people-judgment without permanent headcount growth."},
27	{"id": "p1-026", "text": "Automatically route any cross-team failure with no clear owner to the senior engineer as default owner, so ambiguity supplies new situations on a schedule."},
28	{"id": "p1-027", "text": "Put the engineer's written assessment into every acquisition or partnership diligence memo, named and traceable in board materials."},
29	{"id": "p1-028", "text": "Send the engineer, not a VP, to represent the company at customer executive briefings on technical strategy and roadmap."},
30	{"id": "p1-029", "text": "Give the engineer authority to unilaterally kill or approve vendor contracts based on their own technical assessment, with no executive sign-off required."},
31	{"id": "p1-030", "text": "Connect the engineer's system to three unrelated customers' environments through support or consulting contracts, manufacturing combinatorial complexity no single large-company team faces."}
32	]}

1	{"lens": "inversion", "pool": 3, "items": [
2	{"id": "p3-001", "text": "Give the engineer direct, unreviewed sign-off authority over a named budget or decision class that no manager can override."},
3	{"id": "p3-002", "text": "Assign the single hardest unresolved production problem to the tenured engineer within their first quarter back, not a junior hire."},
4	{"id": "p3-003", "text": "Put the engineer's name, not their manager's, on the incident report or postmortem that circulates to the CEO."},
5	{"id": "p3-004", "text": "Require the engineer present their own system design directly to the executive who controls its budget, no manager relay."},
6	{"id": "p3-005", "text": "Expand the engineer's scope to a second, adjacent system on a fixed 12-month schedule rather than freezing them on one service."},
7	{"id": "p3-006", "text": "Put the engineer in the room for customer escalations tied to code they own, rather than shielding them from customers."},
8	{"id": "p3-007", "text": "Hand the engineer one named problem with a real deadline and full authority over approach, instead of shifting weekly priorities."},
9	{"id": "p3-008", "text": "Let the engineer approve or veto hires onto their own team rather than routing hiring decisions around them."},
10	{"id": "p3-009", "text": "Make the engineer's technical sign-off a hard gate that requires CEO-level escalation to override, not a formality."},
11	{"id": "p3-010", "text": "Assign the most visible cross-team project of the year to the tenured engineer, not to the newest hire."},
12	{"id": "p3-011", "text": "Guarantee the engineer's team headcount or scope grows on a fixed schedule tied to their tenure, immune to the next reorg."},
13	{"id": "p3-012", "text": "Seat the engineer with a vote in the meeting where the roadmap is actually set, not after it is finalized."},
14	{"id": "p3-013", "text": "Have the CEO or CTO personally call the tenured engineer every six months to lay out the next hard problem before recruiters do."},
15	{"id": "p3-014", "text": "Give the engineer a standing discretionary budget for tools, contractors, or small hires up to a fixed dollar cap."},
16	{"id": "p3-015", "text": "Grant an external-facing title reflecting real scope (e.g. 'Head of Payments Infrastructure') that outranks the equivalent big-company title."},
17	{"id": "p3-016", "text": "Put the engineer's name as author on a client-facing technical document or case study, not buried in internal wikis."},
18	{"id": "p3-017", "text": "Route the engineer's reporting line through someone who can demonstrably stretch them technically, verified by a peer review."},
19	{"id": "p3-018", "text": "Attach a visible dollar-impact business metric directly to the engineer's name in company-wide reporting."},
20	{"id": "p3-019", "text": "Let the engineer unilaterally set the architecture standard for their domain rather than routing it through a central committee."},
21	{"id": "p3-020", "text": "Guarantee at least 18 consecutive months on one system before any rotation, so depth compounds instead of resetting."},
22	{"id": "p3-021", "text": "Send the tenured engineer, not a manager, to represent the company as the named technical expert at a customer or industry event."},
23	{"id": "p3-022", "text": "Fund one externally visible technical artifact under the engineer's own byline, such as a public write-up or filed patent, each year."},
24	{"id": "p3-023", "text": "Assign a fixed executive sponsor whose explicit job for two years is to vouch publicly for the engineer's growing scope."},
25	{"id": "p3-024", "text": "Pre-commit, before month 18, a specific harder problem the engineer will own starting month 19."},
26	{"id": "p3-025", "text": "Give the engineer named authority above procurement or legal for technical calls in their domain, so their decisions aren't silently overridden."},
27	{"id": "p3-026", "text": "Staff the team slightly ahead of ticket volume so the tenured engineer gets protected time to build rather than only firefight."},
28	{"id": "p3-027", "text": "Publish the exact external comp benchmark used and set tenured-seat pay a fixed margin above it, not merely at parity."},
29	{"id": "p3-028", "text": "Give the engineer formal veto power over scope-creep requests into the system they own."},
30	{"id": "p3-029", "text": "Brief the tenured engineer directly on strategic bets and risks before any public announcement or layoff news reaches them secondhand."},
31	{"id": "p3-030", "text": "Schedule an authority expansion and an external naming (title, byline, client-facing credit) for every tenured engineer on a fixed 18-month cadence starting day one."}

2	{"id": "p7-001", "text": "Like cleaner wrasse who hold fixed reef stations that client fish return to repeatedly, assign each senior engineer a standing internal 'client' unit whose problems route only through them."},
3	{"id": "p7-002", "text": "Mimic ant-acacia mutualism, where acacia grows hollow thorns and Beltian bodies exclusively for its ant colony: give the engineer a resource (private compute, standing incident authority) accessible nowhere else."},
4	{"id": "p7-003", "text": "As mycorrhizal fungal networks preferentially channel carbon to connected trees, route the org's hardest, most visible problems to senior engineers so internal reputation compounds independent of any employer's brand name."},
5	{"id": "p7-004", "text": "Copy the bobtail squid, which nightly vents and recultures its Vibrio fischeri population: periodically strip and rebuild ownership of a critical system around the same engineer to keep reinstalling their relevance."},
6	{"id": "p7-005", "text": "As salmon imprint on natal-stream chemistry and return to spawn, permanently mark the engineer's original system with their name in architecture records so it stays a homing point."},
7	{"id": "p7-006", "text": "Borrow honeybee swarm quorum sensing, where scouts trigger colony-wide action once a threshold of agreement is reached: let one senior engineer's technical sign-off alone trigger org-wide direction changes."},
8	{"id": "p7-007", "text": "Mirror Florida scrub-jay cooperative breeding, where helpers stay because a bounded breeding territory awaits them: grant the engineer an actual bounded product territory they alone architect, not a title."},
9	{"id": "p7-008", "text": "Like beavers reshaping streams into dams they then must maintain, let the engineer build custom internal tooling only they can operate, making the workplace itself an extension of their own construction."},
10	{"id": "p7-009", "text": "As barnacle cyprid larvae secrete permanent proteinaceous cement bonding irreversibly to a substrate, publish the engineer as sole named architect in an external patent or paper tying their professional identity to this org."},
11	{"id": "p7-010", "text": "Model gall wasps that chemically induce a plant to grow a nutrient-rich chamber sized to the larva inside: redirect resources to build a bespoke structure protecting the engineer's specific project."},
12	{"id": "p7-011", "text": "Like lichen, where fungus and alga cannot survive separately once fused, engineer a technical dependency where the senior engineer's system and a new org capability are mutually inextricable."},
13	{"id": "p7-012", "text": "Copy the fig wasp, obligately paired one species to one fig tree: pair each senior engineer exclusively to one irreplaceable client or system not interchangeable with any other engineer."},
14	{"id": "p7-013", "text": "As albatrosses return across decades to an exact natal nest site, keep continually investing in the original team room or product the engineer started with as a standing symbol tied to them personally."},
15	{"id": "p7-014", "text": "Mimic ant pheromone trail reinforcement, where repeated use strengthens a foraging path: continuously broadcast the engineer's technical wins through a visible internal signal chain so they stay the strongest-marked route others follow."},
16	{"id": "p7-015", "text": "Borrow periodical cicada emergence timing, which overwhelms predators through mass synchrony: synchronize public technical announcements so credit and market visibility pool around the engineer at once, swamping recruiter outreach."},
17	{"id": "p7-016", "text": "As Physarum slime mold prunes weak tubes and reinforces efficient ones in its foraging network, strip bureaucratic steps specifically from the senior engineer's workflow, giving them the shortest decision path in the market."},
18	{"id": "p7-017", "text": "Like weaver ants marking territory with distinct cuticular hydrocarbons that trigger aggression toward outsiders, build idiosyncratic internal tooling and jargon fluent only to insiders, raising the friction of an external move."},
19	{"id": "p7-018", "text": "Mirror elephant matriarchs who alone retain ecological memory of drought-season water sources: make the engineer the official sole holder of undocumented incident history, invoked as a formal standing function."},
20	{"id": "p7-019", "text": "As a Portuguese man o' war colony depends on specialized zooids none of which survive alone, integrate the engineer's module so deeply into other visible systems that its removal visibly cripples them."},
21	{"id": "p7-020", "text": "Copy wolf pack scent-marking of territory boundaries recognized by the whole pack: publicly and repeatedly attribute a named system domain to the senior engineer so others recognize it as theirs."},
22	{"id": "p7-021", "text": "As meerkats rotate a designated sentinel who gains recognized status watching for predators, give the senior engineer a standing, named authority as final technical risk-caller across the org."},
23	{"id": "p7-022", "text": "Like earthworms whose castings progressively condition soil to favor more worms, let the engineer's accumulated simplifications make their current role the objectively easiest place to use their skill, hard to replicate elsewhere."},
24	{"id": "p7-023", "text": "Mirror male weaver birds whose elaborate nests function as a visible fitness signal: have the engineer publicly construct a signature technical artifact kept permanently credited to them inside the org's own records."},
25	{"id": "p7-024", "text": "As the honeyguide bird leads humans to a hive and receives wax after the hive is opened, formalize a reciprocal loop where the engineer flags opportunities and receives a guaranteed cut of what results."},
26	{"id": "p7-025", "text": "Like clownfish that acclimate to anemone nematocysts through gradual mucus-coat exposure, deliberately expose the engineer to the org's internal hazards until only this environment is safe for them at that comfort level."},
27	{"id": "p7-026", "text": "As deep-sea anglerfish males vascularly fuse into the female's body, structure the engineer's compensation as a literal joint ownership stake in a specific product line that cannot be extracted individually."},
28	{"id": "p7-027", "text": "Mimic remora fish attaching to sharks via a modified dorsal sucker disc for free transport and protection: give the engineer a standing seat riding alongside the org's highest-visibility initiatives without separate negotiation each time."},
29	{"id": "p7-028", "text": "As giant clams host zooxanthellae within specialized iridocyte-lined tissue tuned to filter and channel light to the algae, build an internal role tuned exactly to the engineer's specific skill wavelength, unusable elsewhere."},
30	{"id": "p7-029", "text": "Copy octopus arm-level neural autonomy, where each arm solves local problems without central brain approval: grant the engineer standing local authority to resolve decisions in their domain without escalation."},
31	{"id": "p7-030", "text": "Like coral polyps that expel zooxanthellae under stress before the whole colony bleaches, instrument system-level (not survey-based) technical friction signals that trigger a structural fix before the engineer disengages."}
32	]}

Based on the search results, here's what the research shows about cleaner wrasse cleaning stations:

## Fixed Cleaning Stations and Client Fish Behavior

The cleaner wrasse Labroides dimidiatus occupies fixed 'cleaning stations' on coral reefs, which 'client' reef fish visit repeatedly to have parasites removed.

The frequency of these repeat visits is substantial. The most common Indo-Pacific cleaner fish, Labroides dimidiatus, inspects an average 2297 clients day−1 and consumes an average 1218 ectoparasites day−1, with individual clients often cleaned repeatedly, some up to 144 times day−1.

## Types of Client Fish

There are two main types of client fish: visitors and residents. Visitor clients are typically large-bodied species with access to multiple cleaning stations, allowing them to choose among different cleaner fish. In contrast, resident clients are usually smaller, territorial species that rely exclusively on their local cleaning station and have no choice of alternative partners.

## Behavioral Mechanisms

The repeated nature of these interactions enables important behavioral controls. Clients can prevent L. dimidiatus from always cheating using control mechanisms such as chasing and partner switching, which depend on repeated interactions. These control mechanisms would be undermined in the absence of frequent repeated interactions, if cleaners roved over large areas.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about key person clauses in professional services agreements:

## Key Person Clause Overview

The Key Personnel clause identifies specific individuals whose skills or roles are essential to the performance of a contract. It typically requires that these named individuals remain assigned to the project and restricts their replacement without the prior approval of the other party, ensuring continuity and consistency in service delivery.

## Common Components

The clause typically includes the name of the individual that the Company insists will provide the Services, particularly if the Agreement is with a legal entity or business assigned to perform all Services under the Agreement.

Before any Key Personnel are assigned to the Project, the full names and 1-2 page résumés of nominated Key Personnel shall be provided to and approved by Owner.

## Replacement Restrictions

No key personnel substitutions or additions will be made unless necessitated by compelling reasons including illness, death, termination of employment, or family friendly leave, and the contractor must promptly provide required information to the Contracting Officer for approval prior to substitution.

## Termination Rights

In the event that a Customer designates in a Purchase Order that certain individuals are essential to the Services, if such individuals no longer are employed by the Seller, the Customer shall have the right to terminate the Agreement on thirty days' written notice.

These clauses are often included as appendices or exhibits (such as "Attachment F" or schedules) within professional services agreements to formally document the key individuals essential to contract performance.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding individual participation, representative roles, and organizational membership structures in both IETF and W3C:

## W3C Structure

W3C membership is available through Full Member or Affiliate Member agreements. The Advisory Committee is composed of one representative from each Member organization, and the only person who may join a group on behalf of a W3C Member is the Advisory Committee Representative, who then "appoints" participants in the group.

The Advisory Committee representative may designate up to four (or more at the Director's discretion) unpaid agents from the organization who will exercise Membership, and these agents shall disclose their employment affiliation when participating in W3C activities. These agents are expected to represent the broad interests of the W3C Member organization and not the parochial interests of their employers.

For organizational constraints on seats, a Member organization is permitted at most one participant on the TAG and at most one participant on the AB.

## IETF Structure

The IETF operates differently from W3C. The IETF has no concept of membership; anyone who shows up can contribute, and participation in the IETF is considered to be on an individual basis. Everyone understands that you might work for a particular company, but your statements are not representative of them; rather, they are thought of as your statements and opinions.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about engineering blogs and credibility with prospects:

When an engineer sees their name on something they created, they'll be more willing to participate again, which is important for maintaining consistent content. More broadly, content marketing generates qualified leads, shortens your sales cycle because prospects already understand what you do, and builds trust before the first meeting.

Engineering blog posts allow in-house engineering teams to share knowledge and best practices, demonstrate expertise, and allow engineers to speak to what they're working on directly. Additionally, positioning your company as an industry leader helps enhance your brand authority and credibility, and by consistently posting informative and engaging blog posts, customers will view your content as valuable and start to consider you as the go-to expert.

The search results emphasize that engineering posts help peers understand what a particular individual or team within a much larger organization actually works on, keeping sales and marketing to an absolute minimum, which suggests that authentic, engineer-authored content resonates better with developer audiences than heavily marketed material.

Based on the search results, here's what the research shows about cleaner wrasse cleaning stations:

## Fixed Cleaning Stations and Client Fish Behavior

The cleaner wrasse Labroides dimidiatus occupies fixed 'cleaning stations' on coral reefs, which 'client' reef fish visit repeatedly to have parasites removed.

The frequency of these repeat visits is substantial. The most common Indo-Pacific cleaner fish, Labroides dimidiatus, inspects an average 2297 clients day−1 and consumes an average 1218 ectoparasites day−1, with individual clients often cleaned repeatedly, some up to 144 times day−1.

## Types of Client Fish

There are two main types of client fish: visitors and residents. Visitor clients are typically large-bodied species with access to multiple cleaning stations, allowing them to choose among different cleaner fish. In contrast, resident clients are usually smaller, territorial species that rely exclusively on their local cleaning station and have no choice of alternative partners.

## Behavioral Mechanisms

The repeated nature of these interactions enables important behavioral controls. Clients can prevent L. dimidiatus from always cheating using control mechanisms such as chasing and partner switching, which depend on repeated interactions. These control mechanisms would be undermined in the absence of frequent repeated interactions, if cleaners roved over large areas.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about key person clauses in professional services agreements:

## Key Person Clause Overview

The Key Personnel clause identifies specific individuals whose skills or roles are essential to the performance of a contract. It typically requires that these named individuals remain assigned to the project and restricts their replacement without the prior approval of the other party, ensuring continuity and consistency in service delivery.

## Common Components

The clause typically includes the name of the individual that the Company insists will provide the Services, particularly if the Agreement is with a legal entity or business assigned to perform all Services under the Agreement.

Before any Key Personnel are assigned to the Project, the full names and 1-2 page résumés of nominated Key Personnel shall be provided to and approved by Owner.

## Replacement Restrictions

No key personnel substitutions or additions will be made unless necessitated by compelling reasons including illness, death, termination of employment, or family friendly leave, and the contractor must promptly provide required information to the Contracting Officer for approval prior to substitution.

## Termination Rights

In the event that a Customer designates in a Purchase Order that certain individuals are essential to the Services, if such individuals no longer are employed by the Seller, the Customer shall have the right to terminate the Agreement on thirty days' written notice.

These clauses are often included as appendices or exhibits (such as "Attachment F" or schedules) within professional services agreements to formally document the key individuals essential to contract performance.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding individual participation, representative roles, and organizational membership structures in both IETF and W3C:

## W3C Structure

W3C membership is available through Full Member or Affiliate Member agreements. The Advisory Committee is composed of one representative from each Member organization, and the only person who may join a group on behalf of a W3C Member is the Advisory Committee Representative, who then "appoints" participants in the group.

The Advisory Committee representative may designate up to four (or more at the Director's discretion) unpaid agents from the organization who will exercise Membership, and these agents shall disclose their employment affiliation when participating in W3C activities. These agents are expected to represent the broad interests of the W3C Member organization and not the parochial interests of their employers.

For organizational constraints on seats, a Member organization is permitted at most one participant on the TAG and at most one participant on the AB.

## IETF Structure

The IETF operates differently from W3C. The IETF has no concept of membership; anyone who shows up can contribute, and participation in the IETF is considered to be on an individual basis. Everyone understands that you might work for a particular company, but your statements are not representative of them; rather, they are thought of as your statements and opinions.

Based on the search results, I found the relevant information about W3C Advisory Committee representatives and the process for changing them:

The Advisory Committee is composed of one member representative of each W3C member organization. Regarding the process for changing representatives, the AC member is initially that person specified by the member organization in the membership agreement, and may thereafter be changed only in writing (not electronic mail) to the Director.

This information comes from the official W3C ERB Process document, which outlines the formal procedures for W3C member organizations.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about engineering blogs and credibility with prospects:

When an engineer sees their name on something they created, they'll be more willing to participate again, which is important for maintaining consistent content. More broadly, content marketing generates qualified leads, shortens your sales cycle because prospects already understand what you do, and builds trust before the first meeting.

Engineering blog posts allow in-house engineering teams to share knowledge and best practices, demonstrate expertise, and allow engineers to speak to what they're working on directly. Additionally, positioning your company as an industry leader helps enhance your brand authority and credibility, and by consistently posting informative and engaging blog posts, customers will view your content as valuable and start to consider you as the go-to expert.

The search results emphasize that engineering posts help peers understand what a particular individual or team within a much larger organization actually works on, keeping sales and marketing to an absolute minimum, which suggests that authentic, engineer-authored content resonates better with developer audiences than heavily marketed material.
